articles.title_orig: Which Guns And Optics Are Best According To Battle-Tested Ukrainian Soldiers
articles.title_zh: Which Guns And Optics Are Best According To Battle-Tested Ukrainian Soldiers
articles.content_orig:
When it comes to what rifles, sidearms and optics work best in war, there is perhaps no better place to find out than Ukraine. During more than four years of intense defense of their homeland , Ukrainian troops have used an assortment of small arms and accessories, many foreign-made, others domestically produced, to fight the Russians.
To get a better sense of what Ukrainians are currently using on the front lines, what they like, and what they don’t, we reached out to the First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine. The unit is stationed in the bloody Dobropillia sector in the eastern Donetsk region and is in the middle of one of the toughest fights in Ukraine.
Five soldiers from different Azov units with a range of specialties offered their unique insights into the weapons, sights and scopes they like and the ones they don’t.
The soldiers are issued all their weapons exclusively through the brigade’s armaments service, which obtains them from the Ukrainian Defense Ministry (MoD). Individuals, however, told us they sometimes purchase their own sights and scopes and other accessories, depending on the models.
Some of the questions and answers have been slightly edited for clarity.
Tarantino, Chief Armorer, 12th Special Forces Brigade Azov, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine.
When it comes to light weapon systems, the most common is an assault rifle based on the AR-15 [chambered 5.56mm], either domestic production or the one given to us by partner countries.
Chill, Chief Tactical Training Instructor, 41st Unmanned Systems Regiment Pilum, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine .
So, in my personal opinion, the UAR-15 system is better for me because it’s lighter and it’s more reliable. I have worked with both platforms, both systems, and I can compare them based on my experience. And from my personal experience, the AR system is better.
The caliber is 5.56, and it’s also really convenient in terms of its modification and modernization because with the AK platform, you need to adapt it for further adjustments individually. But in the case of the UAR system, it’s really adaptable and you do not basically need anything in order to modernize it or modify it.
Khalepa, Anti-Aircraft Artillery Battery Commander, Air Defense Battalion Strazh, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine.
Well, in our case, we are using larger calibers starting from 12.7mm up to 35mm. So we do not actually use the standard rifles.
Chewie, Deputy Commander for Logistics, Separate Special Operations Detachment Tuman, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine.
When it comes to close combat, usually this is the UAR-15S of Ukrainian manufacturer called Zbroyar.
Barman, Tactical Training Instructor, Personnel Training Battalion, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine.
So currently our key weapon platform is the UAR-15, but previously we also used the AK-74 and other modifications. The AK-74 fires 5.45mm rounds.
Well, the best weapon to work with is not the weapon itself, but the people we are working with. The weapon is only the instrument. But personally, the most reliable weapon is the one that has as few stoppages as possible because the last thing you want is to have a stoppage in the situation where you need to fire.
For me, that is the Heckler & Koch 416 . But I am talking about my preferences and experience. That gun has a gas piston system that has proven itself the most efficient due to the fact that the movement of the piston back and forth is relatively short. That makes the weapon itself much more reliable.
Another system, called DI [ direct impingement used in standard AR-15 pattern rifles], requires much more attention from the gunner who is shooting the rifle. Because in the conditions where the operator, the marksman, is sitting in the trench or in a bunker – especially now in autumn when the humidity is high – this DI system requires much more attention due to the wet weather around. The gas piston system has proven itself much more reliable and it doesn’t need that much attention.
We are using the Ukrainian-manufactured UAR-15 rifle, and you know, as they say, the best rifle is the one that you have.
So the weapon system that I told you about, UAR-15, is indeed the most loved because, in addition to this weapon, we do possess small numbers of Beretta, Bren, and several other weapon systems.
The reason why we prefer the UAR-15 is, first of all, it is much lighter. Second, it’s shorter. Another reason is that, taking into account the combat warfare that we have right now, we have the manufacturer on the premises of our country. It means if something happens to the weapon, it doesn’t take much time to either send the request to the manufacturer for them to send us the spare details, or for us to send the weapon system to them for maintenance.
Our preference is of course the UAR-15, and we’re using the 5.56 UAR platforms because it’s more convenient to use, it’s easier to maintain, and it’s also more reliable. But we also need to understand that our enemy is using the AK platforms, the AK-12 , the AK-74, and while of course we are carrying the 5.56 rounds, usually during the assault actions, we can take the AK rifles and the 5.45 rounds to be able to use our rifles in compatibly with the enemy’s rifles. We can use the AKs for the element of surprise and for deception. The way they look compared to the UAR rifles makes it easier to deceive the enemy.
Well, again, the biggest difference between this gas piston system and the DI system is that the gas piston system has a very short movement back and forth of the piston. It means that the chances of stoppage in this weapon are quite low, while the DI system is much more demanding because these exhaust gases go back into this tube that pushes the bolt carrier back. That means these gases make this tunnel much more dirty. And in a situation when the rotation of the soldier to the battlefield is for two weeks, and these are the two weeks of a very intensive fight, a soldier doesn’t always have the chance to disassemble a weapon and pull the bolt carrier out and clean it.
Compared to the DI system, the Heckler & Koch quality of the barrel itself is exceptionally phenomenal. So the quality of the metal is good, and it allows you to shoot even four or five or even six magazines in a row without the barrel getting overheated.
Well, talking about the piston system, the only AR-15-based rifle which I know has the piston system is the Heckler & Koch 416. So I have some experience in using it, but unfortunately I do not have this rifle. But I would like to. It’s quite reliable based on my communication with other operators and service members. I also get really good feedback about that weapon. But that’s the only weapon system with this piston system that I know of, and yeah, it presents some advantages.
The UAR-15 system that we are currently using within our unit is the DI-based weapon system, and the key difference is that they become contaminated quicker, and they require better and more frequent maintenance, which is not always possible to ensure in combat conditions.
Well, I have served in the infantry since 2022, and I have had some experience with the piston systems, for instance, with the AK system, and I did not really notice any major differences.
We use only the DI system.
Well, from my experience, the gas piston systems like the one that we can find on the HK 416 , they are simpler to maintain. They are more efficient in terms of their principle of operation, and also they are more reliable, I would say.
But the key difference in the DI system is that, of course, it’s a little bit more difficult to maintain them. But at the same time, you can regulate the amount of gas that goes back into the receiver. So, both of these systems have their own advantages and disadvantages.

articles.title_orig: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
articles.title_zh: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age 1 , 2 , 3 . How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested 4 , with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce ) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp ), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp ), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 . Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory 9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.
Europe’s present-day linguistic landscape is dominated by Romance, Germanic and Slavic languages, which expanded relatively recently during the Iron Age 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 . Before these events, Celtic languages were prominent across Europe 1 , 2 , 3 : Lepontic has been documented in northwestern Italy (2600–2100 bp ), Celtiberian in central-northeastern Iberia (2200–1900 bp ) and Gaulish across present-day France, central Europe, northern Italy and the Balkans (2500–1400 bp ) 14 , 15 (Fig. 1a ). In the modern era, Celtic languages have retreated to the northwestern Atlantic fringe, where they persist as two groups: the Goidelic languages Irish, Manx and Scottish Gaelic; and the Brittonic languages Welsh, Cornish and Breton.
a , The four proposed source regions for the spread of the Celtic languages (circled) and the approximate pre-Roman and premodern distribution of Celtic languages from roughly 2000 bp (shaded). b , Tree schematic illustrating the position of Proto-Celtic relative to events that bound its emergence: the divergence of its predecessor (Pre-Celtic) from other Indo-European branches and the subsequent divergence into Brittonic and Goidelic (Insular Celtic). The tree structure and branch lengths are shown for illustrative purposes only and remain unresolved. c , Density plot showing the overlap of estimates for the divergence of Pre-Celtic (computational, quantitative), the emergence and dissolution of Proto-Celtic (archaeological and linguistic, qualitative) and the subsequent divergence of Goidelic and Brittonic (computational, quantitative). The linguistic studies from which the estimates come are depicted in Extended Data Fig. 1 and detailed in Supplementary Table 5.1 . d , e , Geographical ( d ) and temporal ( e ) distributions of ancient samples included in the dataset that overlap with the region and timelines from a and c . In d , a small amount of jitter is added to the geographical coordinates. C. E., central-eastern; N., northern; S., southern; W., western. Base maps in a and d were generated in R (v.4.2.3) using map_data(“world”) in ggplot2 (v.3.5.0.9000); geographic boundary data are derived from the public-domain Natural Earth 1:50 m dataset ( https://www.naturalearthdata.com ) through the R maps package (v.3.4.2.1).
All Celtic languages diverged from an undocumented ancestral language, Proto-Celtic (Fig. 1b,c and Extended Data Fig. 1a ). This language is defined by a series of linguistic innovations present in all Celtic languages, but absent from the other Indo-European languages, including closely related Italic and Lusitanian (Supplementary Note 5 ). Whereas there is widespread agreement that Indo-European dialects, including the one ancestral to Proto-Celtic, spread across Europe from the Pontic Steppe after 5000 bp (refs. 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ), the centre and timing of the subsequent dispersal of Celtic within Europe remain contentious 4 . Existing hypotheses generally fall within one of the following four models:
The Bell Beaker model associates the Celtic split and dispersal with the Late Neolithic to Early Bronze Age Bell Beaker Complex (roughly 4750–4500 to 4000–3800 bp ) 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , which spanned much of western and central Europe. Under this model, Celtic diverged largely in situ over the millennia following the Bell Beaker expansion. By contrast, the following three models place the formation of Proto-Celtic after 4000 bp .
The Celtic-from-the-West model (Fig. 1a ) claims that Proto-Celtic emerged from relatively undiversified Indo-European dialects within long-distance maritime networks of the Atlantic Bronze Age Culture (3300–2700 bp ) 24 , connecting Atlantic Iberia, parts of France, Ireland and Britain. It further posits a subsequent eastward expansion of a Gaulish–Brittonic–Goidelic Celtic subgroup into central Europe during the Hallstatt C period (2750–2600 bp ), traced archaeologically through the distribution of Gündlingen swords 25 .
The Celtic-from-the-Centre model, in turn, posits that Proto-Celtic emerged neither along the Atlantic seaboard nor from eastern central Europe (next model). Instead, it situates this ancestral language in inland France and possibly northwestern Italy 4000–3000 bp , with a subsequent spread in many directions, including to Britain, Italy and Spain, after 3000 bp (refs. 26 , 27 , 28 ) (Fig. 1a ). This model rejects overly strong archaeological–linguistic correlations and is instead supported by a relative density of Celtic toponyms and personal names in France.
Finally, the longstanding Celtic-from-the-East model places the formation of Proto-Celtic in eastern central Europe (Fig. 1a ) and associates its diversification with the Late Bronze Age Urnfield Culture 29 , 30 , the subsequent Hallstatt Culture and La Tène archaeological horizon 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , or a combination of these. The documentation of Lepontic Celtic inscriptions in the Urnfield-derived Alpine Golasecca Culture (2850–2350 bp ) has been taken to support this model 30 . In addition, under this model (as well as models (2) and (3)), the geographic distribution of the Iron Age La Tène Culture, extending from France to the Balkans, broadly coincides with the distribution of Gaulish and closely related Celtic dialects 31 .
These models differ in their proposed centres and chronologies for the formation and spread of Celtic and imply conflicting proposals of human mobility. We therefore test to what degree each model is supported by past population genomic data, similar to approaches that have proved to be illuminative in other historical-linguistic debates 11 , 12 , 16 , 17 , 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 . We note, in this context, that the terms ‘spread’ and ‘population movements’ are used as purely descriptive terms that do not speak to the social mechanism driving them.

articles.title_orig: Bukele’s warning to Haitian gang leaders that his forces will 'finish' them as he did in El Salvador
articles.title_zh: Bukele’s warning to Haitian gang leaders that his forces will 'finish' them as he did in El Salvador
articles.content_orig:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele says his troops will rescue four missing technicians by force if Haitian gangs refuse to hand them over. (Reuters.)
After crushing powerful criminal gangs in El Salvador, President Nayib Bukele has turned his attention to the Caribbean nation of Haiti, deploying 2,000 troops after four Salvadoran military aviation technicians disappeared following an Oct.18 ambush near Port-au-Prince.
"We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too," Bukele wrote in a message on X directed at Haiti's criminal groups. Bukele stressed that the operation's objective was not to invade Haiti or conduct a long-term occupation, but to recover the four missing Salvadorans alive.
The disappearance has become a national priority for Bukele, who has warned Haitian gang leaders that El Salvador is prepared to use overwhelming force if the men are not returned alive.
FLORIDA JURY CONVICTS 4 MEN WHO PLOTTED ASSASSINATION OF HAITI'S PRESIDENT FROM SOUTH FLORIDA HUB
In a screen grab taken from a video released Oct. 29, 2026, soldiers walk across the airport tarmac to board an aircraft after El Salvador's deployment of thousands of troops to Haiti, days after four Salvadoran members of a U.N.-backed force went missing in a gang ambush, in Comalapa, El Salvador. (Handout via Reuters)
The aviation technicians were assigned to a medical unit as part of the United Nations -backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) in Haiti when their armored vehicle was attacked in Croix-des-Bouquets. Haiti’s National Police announced Tuesday, more than two weeks after the attack, that it had found the charred remains of the vehicle in the Santo neighborhood of Croix-des-Bouquets. Police said, however, they found no sign of the missing men.
El Salvador says the men were abducted, the Haitian government says the soldiers are missing, and one gang leader says they are dead.
In a post on X Tuesday, directed at the "Haitian people" and written in Haitian creole, Bukele recalled the 1806 assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who proclaimed Haiti’s independence from France in 1804 and who many regard as the founder of Haiti.
"Dessalines liberated Haiti, but some people who were by his side betrayed him and killed him," Bukele said. "Those traitors still exist in Haiti."
SUSPECTS IN HAITIAN PRESIDENT'S ASSASSINATION TRANSFERRED TO MIAMI, ACCUSED OF FUNDING PLOT WITH COVID FRAUD
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele joined the annual National Prayer Breakfast in Washington, D.C., warning attendees that violent gang members in his country have a documented history of worshiping Satan. (Alex Pena/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Bukele also reposted video of a helicopter engagement in Croix-des-Bouquets.
"Gangs were attacking GSF soldiers from Chad," he wrote. "We arrived quickly and repelled the attackers with our attack helicopters."
Bukele has the backing of President Donald Trump, who, when asked by reporters at Mar-a-Lago on Halloween, confirmed speaking with the Salvadoran president.
"He said that he has a big problem with Haiti," Trump said. "They killed some of his people. I said, 'You're running your country. You have to do what you have to do.'"
Unlike previous foreign interventions, Bukele's deployment has the backing of Haiti's transitional government.
"The international force is not here to replace the state," Haitian Prime Minister Didier Fils-Aimé said Tuesday in his first remarks about the deployment. "They're here to support us."
Fils-Aimé added that Bukele "understands our fight. … He came to stand on the side of the Haitian people."
‘DONROE’ DOCTRINE AND CONSERVATIVE VICTORIES SQUEEZE CARTELS IN LATIN AMERICA
An armored personnel carrier of Haiti's U.N.-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) patrols an area after El Salvador announced a rescue mission for four air force members in the GSF who went missing after a gang ambush in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Oct. 23, 2026. (Patrice Noel/Reuters)
The operation has drawn criticism from human-rights advocates and gang leaders who warn that a military escalation could worsen civilian suffering. The U.N. says at least 5,700 people have been killed or injured due to the gang violence in Haiti since Jan. 1 as security forces struggle to contain the violence.
The U.N. has also indicated that El Salvador’s deployment is separate from the GSF and has warned El Salvador must follow applicable international law.
One of those gang leaders is Wilson Joseph, known as "Lanmò Sanjou," leader of the powerful 400 Mawozo gang. He accused rival gang Chen Mechan of carrying out the ambush and claimed the Salvadorans are dead, he told The Associated Press.
Joseph also sent a letter to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres asking the U.N. for mediation and warning Bukele's "vengeful remarks, expectations, and threats … will lead to an escalation of violence and a logic of reprisals, of which the Haitian people would be the first victims."
EXCLUSIVE: HAITIAN ILLEGAL ALIEN GANG MEMBER WHO WENT VIRAL YELLING ‘BIDEN FOREVER’ DURING ICE ARREST DEPORTED
An armed member of the G9 and Family gang patrols a roadblock in the Delmas 6 neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, March 11. (AP Photo/Odelyn Joseph)
Joseph was indicted by the U.S. in 2022 on hostage-taking charges related to the 2021 kidnapping of 17 missionaries, including 16 Americans, and remains the subject of a reward of up to $1 million for his arrest.
Bukele dismissed such appeals, accusing gang leaders of attempting to use civilians and international concerns about human rights as a shield to preserve their power and avoid accountability. Bukele has said that negotiations have only prolonged the crisis that has devastated Haiti for years.
After years as one of the world's most violent countries, dominated by powerful gangs including MS-13 , El Salvador launched an unprecedented crackdown in 2022 under a state of emergency. Authorities carried out tens of thousands of arrests, ultimately detaining more than 90,000 suspected gang members.
Supporters credit the strategy with driving homicide rates to historic lows and restoring public safety. Critics accuse Bukele's government of human-rights abuses, arbitrary detentions and erosion of due-process protections.
Salvadoran soldiers return to a base after El Salvador deployed thousands of troops to Haiti in response to four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed force that went missing in a gang ambush, in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Oct. 30, 2026. (Patrice Noel/Reuters)
The question now is whether that model can be exported to Haiti, where gangs control large portions of Port-au-Prince and wield influence over key transportation routes and neighborhoods. Despite years of international intervention, security conditions have continued to deteriorate.
The GSF has struggled with manpower shortages and operational limitations, operating below its Security Council-approved intended strength, leaving Haiti's government unable to reassert full control over much of the capital.

"We can help you defeat them, but we are not your enemies," Bukele wrote on Tuesday. "We must stand up, take back control of our communities, and put under our control those who are making us endure all this pain, all this suffering. We are right there beside you… Haiti will be free."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Soars 1,500 Points As At Least 10 Stocks Break Out (Live Coverage)
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Soars 1,500 Points As At Least 10 Stocks Break Out (Live Coverage)
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. stock market surged on Wednesday as investors digested the impact of the Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm congressional elections.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared more than 1,500 points or 2.9% in afternoon trading, putting the blue-chip index on track for its biggest gain of the year. The broader S&P 500 rose 1.7% while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index gained 1.8%.
The shifting political winds could affect a range of issues that influence investment returns, from the pace of the data center buildout and cryptocurrency industry regulation to proposals to cap credit card interest rates.
At the same time, Wall Street analysts do not expect the outcome to derail a stock market being driven more by robust corporate profits and solid economic growth than by politics.
"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown of Capital Economics said in a note to investors.
Stocks of solar-power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans.
Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Mr. Trump's social media company, the artificial intelligence sector and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans. Trump Media & Technology's stock price fell nearly 17% in afternoon trading, while shares of Musk-owned SpaceX and Tesla sank 3.4% and 2%, respectively.
Investors also expect the election results to heighten gridlock in Congress, with Democratic lawmakers now in control of both the House and Senate, and Mr. Trump threatening to wield his veto power to block any legislation he opposes.
Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress' ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing the risk of volatility, according to Wall Street analysts.
Meanwhile, stocks have generally performed well following midterm elections. The S&P 500 stock index rose an average of 15.5% in the six months after the last 14 midterm races, dating back to 1970, according to figures from investment firm Edward Jones.
"Economic growth, inflation, interest rates and corporate earnings have historically mattered more to broad investment performance than the party composition of Congress, especially if the president and congressional leadership come from different parties," analysts with the Wells Fargo Investment Institute said in a report.
"We do not expect sweeping policy changes," they added. "More likely, in our view, is a split-government alignment on affordability, energy policy and opportunities from artificial intelligence."
Beyond the Beltway, the midterm electoral results could affect key issues for investors, such as the pace of data center construction, with enormous spending on artificial intelligence helping drive stocks to record highs this year while also raising concerns about a bubble in tech stocks .
"In divided government, the policy implications at the federal level may be limited, but data center policy decisions sit at the state and utility-commission level, making gubernatorial and utility races important alongside Congress, particularly Governor Abbott's loss in Texas," Jeff Buchbinder of LPL Research told investors.
"LPL Research continues to expect the buildout to occur, but strong performances by Democrats in key data center states (and pushback from the 'not in my backyard' folks) may slow it down some, potentially increasing regulatory pressure on AI infrastructure stocks including semiconductors, machinery and power generation," he added.

For more options-trading reaction to the rally, click the link at the top of the page for Options Action LIVE featuring CNBC contributors Michael Khouw and Brent Kochuba alongside host Oliver Renick.
Stocks are surging after midterms brought a Democratic blue wave and options traders are responding by selling volatility and embracing a rotation away from big-tech trades. The S&P 500 added just shy of 2% by midday Wednesday, recovering losses from Friday and Monday. The move in its corresponding options prices was even bigger, with the Cboe Volatility index falling about four points to below 17, the biggest one-day drop in the volatility gauge since at least July. Crude oil prices fell as WTI traded below $90 and energy stocks dropped 5.6% for the biggest decline in the S&P 500. Options on the State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE) jumped to more than three times the 30-day average, with 57% puts by volume and the big-money trades concentrated in bearish put-buyers. The top trade in XLE was the 62.5-strike put expiring Jan. 15, suggesting it could be a slow rollover for what has been the best-performing sector of 2026, SpotGamma data show. With the drop in crude oil, a handful of inflation and interest-rate related trades got some bullish attention. Consumer discretionary stocks rallied almost 5% but options volume in the SPDR sector fund XLY was below average and volume was split between puts and calls, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Instead, there was some big action in a few housing trades such as Rocket Companies , the mortgage lender and Redfin owner that fell almost 50% this year before turning around last month. Options volume on Rocket was double the average with a strong bullish bias. Of the 110,000 options traded, 90% were calls and more were likely initiated by buyers than sellers. Bulls traded the bulls like the 14 and 16-strike calls expiring Nov. 20 the most. Opposite the drop in crude oil was a rally in solar energy companies, extending recent gains and extending unusual options activity that preceded the midterms. The Invesco Solar ETF (TAN) added another 9%, trading the highest since July. Options volume was more than five times the average and 80% of the volume was in calls. The most popular trade in TAN was the 48-strike call betting on a 6% rally through Nov. 20th. On the tech side, options flows looked bearish in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) , which fell 2.6% to the lowest since May. Options volume was twice the average, 70% of it puts, with the 475-strike put expiring Nov. 13 the most popular contract bought by volume.

No matter how thoroughly you brush your teeth in the morning and evening, the battle against bacteria is almost certain to be lost.
Within a few hours of brushing, it will return in force and rebuild a solid defence line on the surface of your teeth.
From ancient times to now, humanity has essentially had only one way of dealing with it, whether it was using twigs and sticks or the first bristled toothbrushes, which date back to 10th century China.

Xbox Cloud Gaming is getting a phone controller and new direct Wi-Fi connectivity for the Xbox Nano.
Xbox Cloud Gaming is getting a phone controller and new direct Wi-Fi connectivity for the Xbox Nano.
I revealed yesterday that the new Xbox Nano controller supports a Wi-Fi connection directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming, and now Microsoft is making it official today. Two new Xbox previews will let players try out using a phone as a controller on smart TVs, as well as cloud connect on the Xbox Nano to connect directly to cloud servers.
“Instead of a Bluetooth connection to your TV, cloud connect uses your Wi-Fi to connect directly to the cloud server running your game,” says the Xbox team . “That can help reduce input latency, so gameplay may feel more responsive.”
Players in the US will be able to preview the new cloud connect option for the Xbox Nano controller starting today. If you’re not in the US you will be able to preview a new phone controller option on smart TVs. The controller is available on the Xbox Cloud Gaming website, allowing people to use the streaming service without a dedicated Bluetooth controller.
Microsoft says “both experiences are still being tested” and that “availability and supported games or devices may be limited” during this beta phase. You’ll need to use the Xbox beta app for Android or the Xbox Accessories app on PC to set up cloud connect on the Nano controller, and the smart TV phone controller just requires a toggle of preview features from the Settings > Account section of Xbox Cloud Gaming.

Fox News' Stephanie Bennett reports on the escalations, which have left hundreds of officers injured. Demonstrators burn down a century-old town hall in Limoges as Macron calls for calm amid the worsening nationwide unrest.
The U.S. Embassy has issued an urgent security alert for Americans in France, warning travelers to brace for severe disruptions, sudden curfews and the potential for violence as a massive nationwide strike threatens to paralyze the country on Thursday, Nov. 5.
Beyond widespread shutdowns affecting public transit, schools and healthcare, authorities warn that recent demonstrations have already escalated into property destruction and looting.
With France's four largest railway unions joining the multi-sector walkout, unapproved protests are expected to spill outside planned routes through the weekend.
LOUVRE TURNS AWAY TOURISTS AS PARIS BRACES FOR RENEWED VIOLENCE FOLLOWING DESTRUCTIVE RIOTS
In response, local officials are implementing strict, short-notice curfews that restrict free movement and block access to public landmarks in major areas , including Paris and its surrounding neighborhoods.
The strike comes as unions demand higher wages, better working conditions and increased funding for public services, according to reports.
Americans traveling to France are being warned to prepare for widespread disruptions as a nationwide strike threatens to affect transportation. (Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images)
Travelers could face disruptions to trains and other public transportation as demonstrations take place across the country.
The embassy warned Americans to avoid protests and large gatherings, noting that recent demonstrations have turned violent and included property damage and looting.
Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. Embassy for comment and further details.

Violent demonstrations in October prompted localized curfews in several cities, while riot police used tear gas near Place de la République in Paris as clashes unfolded, Fox News Digital previously reported.
People walk by looted shops after a day of violent clashes between police and protesters amid rising tension over rising living costs, fuel prices and education funding in Paris, France, on Oct. 18, 2026. (Hesham Elsherif/Anadolu/Getty Images)
The unrest also affected some of the country's best-known tourist attractions.

Riot police officers run across a street during protests in Paris, France, on Oct. 17, 2026. (Bruno Camillo/Reuters)
With more demonstrations expected, the U.S. Embassy warned that protest routes could change and gatherings may take place outside areas approved by authorities.

articles.content_orig:

Shares of Lumentum (LITE) fell 18.6% on Monday, November 2, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.5%. That morning, Lumentum and Marvell Technology announced an agreement for Marvell to buy Lumentum in an all-stock deal. An earnings calendar also listed a Lumentum quarterly report for November 2. Lumentum did report that day, and Zacks put its quarterly earnings at $4.57 a share, above the $4.22 consensus. What does the deal give Lumentum shareholders, and how did investors take it?
What Marvell Agreed To Pay For Lumentum
The companies said Lumentum shareholders will receive a fixed 4.500 shares of Marvell common stock for each Lumentum share they own. They put the deal's implied enterprise value, which counts debt as well as shares, at $115 billion. That figure works out to about $1,132 per Lumentum share, which matches 4.500 times Marvell's $251.65 close on October 28, before talks were reported. At Marvell's $171.41 close on Monday, the 4.500 shares were worth about $771, against Lumentum's $684.40 close. Because the payment is in Marvell shares rather than cash, what a Lumentum holder receives rises and falls with Marvell's stock.
Shares of both companies fell on Monday after Marvell announced the agreement, and news reports said shareholders of both companies panned the deal. Marvell fell 12.7%, which cut the value of the stock Lumentum holders are set to receive. Earlier news reports on October 29 said Marvell was in talks to buy Lumentum. The stock rose 0.6% that day before dropping 8.6% on Friday, October 30.
Marvell is buying a fast-growing maker of optical-networking technologies. Lumentum's revenue reached $1.01 billion in fiscal Q4 2026, the quarter ended June 27, up 109.3% from a year earlier. In the quarter it reported on November 2, revenue rose 136.5% to $1.26 billion. On its August 11 call, management said it had begun shipping its faster 1.6T cloud transceivers and was still shipping behind customer demand for its laser chips.
Did Lumentum Fall With Other Tech Stocks?
Only partly. The SPDR technology sector ETF (XLK) fell 2.9% during the same session, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1.1%. Four of the five companies on Lumentum's Trefis peer list also fell, including Cisco Systems, which dropped 2.8%. F5 fell further, losing 4.1%. Those declines were small next to Lumentum's, so most of its fall was its own.
Where Lumentum Stock Stands After The Fall
Lumentum had no fall this large in the prior 365 days, with its only move of this size in that time being a 23.6% rise on November 5, 2025. Over the twelve months to November 2, the stock still returned 242.0%, against 11.8% for the S&P 500.
Trading over the past month has run the other way. The shares closed at their highest level of the year, $1,133.40, on October 6, 2026. Over the month to November 2, the stock lost 36.9% , while the S&P 500 lost 2.3%.
Still Holding Lumentum After The Drop?
Selling a fallen stock can still bring a tax bill if you bought long ago, and holding keeps the risk. A free 30-minute strategy review with our partner advisory firm covers a floor under a large position and a lower-tax unwind.

Trump Media stock and WLFI coin saw declines but he is still $2.7bn wealthier than when he won election in 2024
Donald Trump ’s wealth is falling along with his political fortunes.
Tradable investment assets that helped make the president more than $2bn during his first year in office are collapsing in value the day after the Democrats trounced the Republicans in the midterm elections . Trump Media and Technology Group stock, which trades on the Nasdaq exchange, was priced at just over $5 on Wednesday morning – its lowest mark ever, and down from an all-time high of $101. It lost 11% overnight, dropping from $5.90 once the election returns started coming in. Trump has reported he owns 114m shares of DJT.
Trump owns over 40% of the stock through a trust. He has still grown his wealth dramatically during his presidency; Forbes estimated in a September analysis that he is $ 2.7bn wealthier than when he won the White House in 2024.
Another major asset for Trump and his family are World Liberty Financial digital tokens . The digital coins are trading at less than 5 cents after the election. At their height, in 2025, they were valued at six times that, at 31 cents. The WLFI coin, the governance token of World Liberty financial, began sliding in late October as the election drew near, and as a hack of Binance rattled crypto markets. It experienced a steep decline around 7pm ET on Tuesday as polls in some states closed.
Trump already made more than $500m in profit selling crypto assets last year, according to his personal financial disclosures, though he still owns 15bn tokens.
World Liberty is a venture created by the Trump family and the family of Steven Witkoff. Trump appointed Witkoff, a personal friend and real estate developer, to negotiate diplomatic arrangements about Gaza, Iran and Ukraine.
The value of both WLIF and DJT has always been pegged to the way Trump is perceived, said Jim Angel, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business.
“People think they’re investing in Trump. They really aren’t. They’re really betting on his popularity. That’s what they’re betting on.
“Right now his popularity is at record lows,” Angel added, “and so we see the price of DJT and World Liberty at record lows.”
Separate digital novelty coins called $Trump , which made the president $636m in sales in 2025, have also collapsed in value. They are priced at about $1.40 and seem to have lost about 10% of their value overnight as election results came in. They launched shortly before his inauguration and briefly traded as high as $45 in January 2025.
World Liberty Financial, the Trump and Witkoff crypto company, also issues a so-called stablecoin, USDI1, and the Trump administration recently gave the company a banking license. The stablecoins are pegged to the US dollar and do not fluctuate dramatically.

articles.title_orig: CVS to break up $117 billion business, separating pharmacies from insurance; shares fall
articles.title_zh: CVS to break up $117 billion business, separating pharmacies from insurance; shares fall
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health plans to break itself up — and this time, the bet looks a lot more viable.
The healthcare conglomerate on Wednesday announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. CVS would separate its pharmacy business – including roughly 9,000 retail locations – from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark.
The move comes more than two years after CVS considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea. At the time, analysts questioned whether the retail pharmacy business could survive on its own.
“Back then, the idea of retail standing alone was unthinkable,” Brian Tanquilut, senior equity research analyst at Jefferies, told CNBC.
But the economics of the businesses have changed: CVS's retail pharmacy business has become more consistently profitable, while its insurer, Aetna, has improved its performance despite persistently high medical costs in Medicare Advantage plans. That could make it easier for the company to separate the units — and for investors to recognize the value of each on its own, rather than valuing them together as one sprawling healthcare conglomerate.
“For us, it's showing the stability of the pharmacy,” Michael Cherny, senior research analyst at Leerink Partners, said in an interview. “This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome.”
CVS CEO David Joyner told CNBC’s "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that back in 2024, the company was "in a turnaround" without the flexibility, cash or business performance to execute a split. Now, CVS has posted eight consecutive quarters of beating Wall Street earnings estimates and has raised its guidance several times over the last two years, thanks to improvement across its PBM, pharmacy and insurer.
Since taking the helm in 2024, Joyner has pursued an aggressive turnaround plan that involves $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
The company also now expects to generate at least $15.5 billion in operating cash flow in 2026, a roughly 70% increase from $9.1 billion in 2024, and says it has reached its leverage target ahead of schedule.
"What's changed in two years is the fact that we now can look at this business and the assets that are assembled and really determine, without any distress or without anything that we have to do, what is the right strategic decision to make," Joyner told analysts on a call Wednesday, adding that the decision comes "out of strength."
While investors have largely cheered CVS's progress in recent years, Wall Street appeared more pessimistic about Wednesday's announcement, as the company's shares dropped about 12%.
CVS's retail business has benefited from changes in the competitive landscape, including the widespread retrenchment and store closures of Walgreens, Rite Aid and other pharmacy operators over the last few years. That’s created opportunities for CVS to gain market share, some analysts told CNBC.
CVS has also introduced changes to its pharmacy reimbursement model. Its CostVantage program is designed to replace the traditional process with a more transparent, cost-based model. Some analysts say that has helped the company better align reimbursement with the cost of dispensing prescriptions and contributed to steadier profits.
Those developments represent a meaningful shift for a business that has faced years of pressure from declining prescription reimbursement, store closures and competition from online pharmacies and other retailers.
That doesn't mean the retail pharmacy has become a high-growth business. CVS's retail pharmacy segment remains a relatively low-margin operation, with adjusted operating margins of roughly 4% to 5%. But analysts say it may now be stable and profitable enough to operate independently – even if investors value it at a discount to CVS's other businesses.
In a note Wednesday, RBC Capital Markets analyst Ben Hendrix said the lower valuation investors assign to the retail pharmacy unit has weighed on CVS's overall value and obscured the earnings strength of businesses like Aetna and Caremark.
The underlying growth of the insurance and PBM businesses is also stronger than that of retail pharmacy, Tanquilut said, after accounting for changes to Caremark's rebate arrangements.
Aetna in particular has gotten a better handle on medical costs by exiting unprofitable markets, expanding value-based care models, and tightening utilization management.
The breakup also comes as Caremark faces mounting scrutiny over PBM practices, including state-level legal and regulatory challenges involving the businesses and their relationships with pharmacies.
Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban any one company from owning both a pharmacy and a PBM — thought the Arkansas measure has been held up in court. Cherny noted that legal hurdles involving PBMs in other states have continued to pile up.
“Through what seems to be a never-ending litany of state lawsuits, it feels like it's been under more pressure,” Cherny said. “It's unclear if it just became, for lack of a better term, too tenuous to move forward with those two entities combined as one. I’m not sure.”
Even so, Joyner told the Wall Street Journal that the company wasn’t splitting up because of regulatory issues. CVS has said the separation follows a strategic review and is intended to give each business greater focus and flexibility.
The move also marks a significant departure from the integrated healthcare strategy CVS spent years building.
CVS spent roughly $70 billion to acquire Aetna in 2018 and argued that combining health insurance, pharmacy benefit management, retail pharmacies and health providers under one roof would help coordinate care and create a competitive advantage. CVS was still promoting that model as recently as its investor day last year.
The proposed split suggests the company now sees more value in separating at least some of those businesses – though it is not abandoning vertical integration altogether.
Aetna and Caremark will remain together in the healthcare company, alongside CVS’s specialty pharmacy, its primary care clinic Oak Street Health and its home-visit provider Signify Health. The separate pharmacy company will include roughly 9,000 retail stores, mail pharmacy operations and MinuteClinic, a retail medical clinic located inside certain CVS locations.
Both sides are large enough that they can stand on their own, Cherny said. Caremark is one of the country's three largest PBMs, while CVS has one of the largest retail pharmacy footprints in the U.S.
But separating the company raises questions about how much of the commercial relationship between the businesses can survive.
The relationship has historically benefited both sides. As it stands, Caremark can use CVS's extensive retail footprint to offer members convenient access to prescriptions and steer them toward CVS locations through preferred pharmacy arrangements. Programs such as Maintenance Choice, for example, give eligible members the option to fill certain maintenance medications at CVS retail pharmacies or through mail order.
Those arrangements also helped direct prescription volume to CVS's stores, giving the retail pharmacy unit an important source of customers. Because the businesses shared a parent company, the financial benefits of that relationship ultimately went to CVS as a whole.
In a note, RBC's Hendrix also raised questions about how the split could impact Aetna's Medicare Advantage quality ratings, which determine whether health plans qualify for bonus payments from the government. Retail pharmacists have played a role in engaging Aetna members, and a separation could complicate that relationship.

articles.title_orig: Oil Prices Sink as U.S. Midterms Raise Market Hopes for Middle East Solution
articles.title_zh: Oil Prices Sink as U.S. Midterms Raise Market Hopes for Middle East Solution
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices fell on Wednesday in a volatile session ​as investors awaited Washington's next move in ​the US-Israeli war on ​Iran, after Democrats captured control of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republicans in the midterm elections.
Brent futures fell 2.5% to $101.02 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 2.6% to $93.61.
In the previous session, Brent settled at its lowest level in ⁠nearly four weeks as traders weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
President Donald Trump acknowledged that the US-Israeli war on Iran played a role in his party's sweeping defeat in the midterm elections, as Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.
"President ‌Trump's conflicting signals, with military strikes continuing alongside statements downplaying further escalation, have made it difficult for traders to build strong directional conviction," said Priyanka Sachdeva, head of market insights at Phillip Nova, adding ​that profit-taking and a reduction in speculative long positions were justified after the sharp rally in October.
The US had carried out "defensive" strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said on Tuesday.
Markets remained on watch for any progress in talks to end the US-Israeli war with ⁠Iran, as Qatar stepped up mediation efforts to avert an escalation of attacks after the US elections. A senior Iranian official told Reuters ‌on Tuesday that Iran and the United States remain far from a deal ‌to end their war.
US President Donald Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that the United States had no immediate plans to strike Iran.
Meanwhile flows of crude, condensate and refined products, excluding LPG, averaged 17.1 million barrels per day in October, according to ship-tracking data ⁠from Vortexa, marking a drop from 18.9 million bpd in September but still representing roughly three-quarters of pre-war ⁠levels.
"The continued recovery in crude shipments from the Middle East has begun to weigh on physical ⁠cargo prices, potentially helping to accelerate the normalisation of refining margins and, ultimately, lower fuel prices," said Saxo Bank analyst Ole Hansen.
"However, for consumers to feel the full benefit, refined product exports ​from Middle Eastern refineries must also recover. So far, this ‌is one area where the rebound in flows remains notably subdued, suggesting that relief at the pump may take longer to materialise."
In the US, crude stocks fell by 5.27 million barrels in the week ended October 30, market sources said on Wednesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Eight analysts polled by Reuters had expected, on average, a rise of about 880,000 barrels in crude ​inventories.
Official data from the US Energy Information Administration is ‌due at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
articles.title_zh: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
A trio of smartphone developers want to bring back the compact phone with a 5.3-inch Android 17 device slated to first arrive next May.
The project is called “Enough phone,” and comes from Austin Boer, Brennan Jordan, and William Stults, who are working to create a “premium, small smartphone” similar in size to the iPhone 12 mini. “After years of watching phones get bigger and bigger, we decided it was time for the return of the small smartphone!” the group says.
On Wednesday, the group launched their Kickstarter campaign to raise their goal of $250,000 in funding, after documenting their efforts to use a factory in China to build the device. The aim is to sell the product for $599, although early backers can receive the first batch of models starting at $399.
Currently, many of the best small phones are larger, with a 6.1-inch or 6.3-inch screen size, which can be a little unwieldy if you have small hands. The Enough phone promises to fill the gap with a device that promises to be “comfortable to use with one hand,” the trio said in their initial announcement . One member runs a “dumbphone” business in Dumbwireless, the other two manage Sleke, the maker of OdysseyOS, known as a “De-Googled Android With No Browser.”
The group has already created a non-working prototype and released the device’s “target specs,” which include using a MediaTek Dimensity 7500 processor, 8GB of RAM, 128GB of storage, and a 1,520 by 720 resolution LCD Display, The specs are a bit underwhelming, considering the competition from more established vendors offering cutting-edge components. But the trio says the Enough phone is also meant to be a more minimal device, hence the name.
“Most phones are built to keep you engaged: big screens, built for gaming, streaming, and scrolling. Enough phone is built the other way: The screen is large enough for messages, maps, photos and music, and small enough to be easily put down,” the Kickstarter campaign says. The Enough phone will also come with a removable 3,500 mAh battery, and software updates are planned through 2032.
I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector.
Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service.
I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard.
I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

articles.title_orig: American Voters Overwhelmingly Reject AI Data Centers
articles.title_zh: American Voters Overwhelmingly Reject AI Data Centers
articles.content_orig:
People across America rejected data centers during last night’s midterm election. Proposals related to data centers were explicitly on the ballot in more than 40 races across 13 states. People voted against data centers in 38 of them and counting. Six cities voted to ban data centers outright and 12 put limits on the amount of megawatts such buildings could draw. In addition to specific ballot measures, candidates who supported data centers lost across the country.
One of the most striking repudiations of pro data center politicians was in Texas, where Gregg Abbott lost a bid for a fourth term as governor. Abbott had made Texas a data center friendly place. The state has more than 300 working data centers and there are plans to double that number . “Texas is the epicenter of AI development,” Abbott said in 2025 at a press conference with Google CEO Sundar Pichai. “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.” He went on to accept more than $9 million from data center-related donors .
When public sentiment turned against data centers, Abbott attempted to ride shifting political winds by issuing a “pause” on new projects. The pause wasn’t real. Texas regulators continued to approve data center projects after Abbott’s announcement and only shut down the state’s permitting web portal when 404 Media reported it.
Gina Hinojosa, Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, made Abbott’s stance on data centers a central part of her campaign. Abbott’s words about making Texas a data center-friendly AI state played on TVs and the internet over and over again. He lost by more than 700,000 votes.
Anti-data center candidates overwhelmingly won statewide races across the country. In Burgin, Kentucky, mayoral candidate George Hensley lost his bid after voting to approve a hyperscale project—to a write-in candidate. Hensley was the only name on the ballot, and he lost to Joe MonroeTK, who ran an anti-data center write-in campaign. Emporia, Kansas — where police arrested a school teacher for clapping during a data center related city meeting — passed a ban on high impact data centers. In Yukon, Oklahoma the mayor lost a recall election after he supported a hyperscale data center project .
"These midterms sent a clear message — people don't want to see data centers in their backyards,” Michael Whitesides, the deputy communications director for Local Progress , told 404 Media. “Across the country, people do not see the promised benefit of these data centers, and the AI they power, playing out in their daily lives. They're seeing basic goods and services get more expensive while these billionaire backed monstrosities take up space in their community, poison their air, and drive up their utility bills.”
Local Progress is a network of local elected officials. Over the past year, its members have become increasingly focused on data centers as a top political issue. “Last night, we saw local, state, and federal officials who backed data center deals lose their seats,” Whitesides said. He noted that Kim Rooney in Asheville, North Carolina and Amanda Rodrigues in San Marcos, Texas (both members of Local Progress) were elected mayors in their cities after running anti-data center campaigns.
“Big Tech will continue its typical playbook of trying to buy and bully local officials into complying with their demands for more data center development, but our hope is that last night's results are a clear signal to local leaders that they can resist and their community will back them up,” Whitesides said.
American voters in the communities where they’re being built hate data centers. They run up power bills, burn through water, and power Silicon Valley’s  AI apparatus. America rejected data centers last night as both symbols of the big tech oligarchy and a physical manifestation of the future it wants to build. It’s a future Americans seem willing to fight.
Elon Musk, one of the night’s big losers, took a break from a weeks-long posting spree on X as the election results rolled in. Musk spent half a billion dollars on the midterms, $224 of it in Texas, the state where he lives and does a lot of business. The world’s richest man wanted to cover the state in data centers. Those plans aren’t looking good now that Abbott is out and Hinojoa is in.
Musk broke his election day posting silence a little after 1 am. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he said on X. Chased off the land by its people, the billionaire looks to the sky.

articles.title_orig: ‘Enough Phone’ is an Android phone roughly the size of iPhone 13 Mini, launching in 2027
articles.title_zh: ‘Enough Phone’ is an Android phone roughly the size of iPhone 13 Mini, launching in 2027
articles.content_orig:
Everyone says they want small Android phones back, and 2027 might be your chance to actually buy one. The “Enough Phone” has a mere 5.3-inch display, decent specs, and a price of $599 and less.
Launching in May 2027, the “Enough Phone” is a 5.3-inch Android phone that simply does want to be “enough.”
The company says the 5.3-inch LCD display comes in at 1520×720 and that the phone will be powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chipset, 8GB of RAM, and offers 128GB of storage. It’ll come with either “stock Android” or OdysseyOS, an Android skin used by SLEKE and designed to be minimal and act like a modern dumbphone. SLEKE currently sells repurposed Pixel phones running this software.
Android 17 will run out of the box with updates through 2032.
“Enough Phone” measures in at 132.8 x 63.8 x 12mm and will have a battery between 3,500 and 4,000 mAh which will be user-replaceable. While it’s thicker, the physical size is roughly the same as iPhone 13 Mini.
Rounding out the package would be a fingerprint sensor in the power button, a single 50MP (Sony IMX766) camera on the back, and a 32MP selfie camera up front.
The company says that these specs are “mostly final” and that pricing is planned for $599.
“Enough Phone” is funding on Kickstarter with $399, $449, and $499 early bird reservation tiers ahead of the May 2027 shipping estimate.

articles.title_orig: Trump can't pack the Fed board with allies now
articles.title_zh: Trump can't pack the Fed board with allies now
articles.content_orig:
Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory , and particularly their coming control of the US Senate, strengthen the Federal Reserve against President Trump’s efforts to meddle with it, with the Senate’s control over appointments a major guardrail against Trump landing any more allies at the central bank.
It could also mean new headaches for Chairman Kevin Warsh, with key oversight committees now in the hands of Democrats, and in the case of the Senate Banking Committee, with Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, of Massachusetts, a harsh Warsh critic , likely replacing Trump ally and Warsh supporter Tim Scott of South Carolina as the panel’s chair.
Warsh “got no support for his chairmanship from Democrats … Hostile questioning could put Warsh’s rhetoric to the test,” as he pursues a quieter and less publicly transparent form of central banking, economists from Monetary Policy Analytics, the firm of former Fed Governor Larry Meyer, wrote about the fallout of a Democratic Senate win.
Democrats, having campaigned heavily on cost-of-living issues, have incentive to push Warsh on the central bank’s inflation mandate , while the panel will have broad room to investigate issues they regard as important — such as, in Warren’s case, Warsh’s opaque disposition of hundreds of millions of dollars in assets as he ascended to the Fed’s top job.
For Trump, the new dynamics on Capitol Hill directly stymie his effort to put more allies on the Fed’s seven-member board, three of whom were appointed by former President Joe Biden. Former Chair Jerome Powell, appointed to consecutive terms by Trump and Biden but now at odds with the president, remains on the board as well.
The president has called the configuration “hostile” and “partisan,” and argued the Fed needs to drastically cut interest rates that policymakers — including Warsh — have instead been raising to control high inflation.
Trump’s effort to fire Governor Lisa Cook remains ongoing, with a White House administrative procedure expected in coming weeks to set the stage for a Trump announcement that he has “cause” to fire her over errors on mortgage applications that predate her appointment to the Fed.
A court challenge is likely to follow. The Supreme Court has ruled against Trump once already on the effort to oust Cook, and there’s next to no prospect he would get a chosen replacement confirmed by a Democrat-led Senate if he were ultimately successful in removing her.
Even a Republican-controlled body rejected what were seen as extreme Fed appointments during Trump’s first term, and earlier this year Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who decided not to run for reelection in North Carolina after Trump threatened him in a race won by Democrat Roy Cooper on Tuesday, held up Warsh’s nomination until the administration abandoned a criminal investigation of Powell .
A Senate under Democratic control “would change the confirmation environment for future Trump nominees…and could provide the Fed with a different degree of political support,” Mark Spindel, a partner at Pilot Wave Holdings and author of a book about Fed politics, wrote in an analysis of the election’s implications.
Fed independence “has always depended in part on Congress, and institutional support from the Senate can affect how much room policymakers have to make decisions based on inflation and employment rather than political pressures.”
Democratic control of the Senate committee as well as the House Financial Services Committee could also entangle the bank and regulatory reforms pushed by the administration and by current Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman, with the Fed drafting rules over things like the Genius Act regulating stablecoins, and Bowman recently rolling out a consolidation of the Fed’s bank supervision system.

articles.title_orig: CVS to Split Off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
articles.title_zh: CVS to Split Off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate breakups in history, the company announced Wednesday.
The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs.
The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release . Shares of CVS fell more than 12% on Wednesday.
It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shake-ups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
But Joyner told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday that the decision to split is "out of a position of strength," pointing to recovery in Aetna's Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy.
"So it's all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company," he later added.
CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion.
The two new companies would both be publicly traded.
The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said.
Existing CVS shareholders will own stock in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans.
The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and the healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion.
CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period.
Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's healthcare benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year.
On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business.
CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits.
It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units.
But Joyner told CNBC that the company was "in a turnaround" at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split.
In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows "the stability of the pharmacy," which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent.
"This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome," he told CNBC on Wednesday.
One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers.
But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses "are going to be preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations," adding that "we don't need the integration of an operating structure."
Cherny said the rationale for the split could also extend to the state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration.
The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban co-ownership of PBMs and pharmacies. Those have been challenged in court by CVS and other companies.
PBMs have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies.

articles.title_orig: Jokes fly as Trump’s DJT stock plummets to Happy Meal prices
articles.title_zh: Jokes fly as Trump’s DJT stock plummets to Happy Meal prices
articles.content_orig:
On Wednesday, following the GOP’s historic midterm bloodbath , President Donald Trump received another humiliation when the price of his signature DJT stock plunged to its lowest point ever. While investors were once paying $175 per share, it’s worth just over $5 as of this writing, or as the internet noted , “about as much as a Happy Meal.”
DJT is the stock ticker for Trump Media & Technology Group Corp. (TMTG), the parent company for Trump’s Truth Social social media platform. Launched in 2021, early investors paid as much as $175 per share, which plunged to about $13 per share within two years. After the company went public in 2024 amidst Trump’s presidential campaign, its value briefly jumped to $61.96 but has been falling off ever since, and has been in freefall since October. Then on Election Day, as it became clear that the Republicans had been decimated by the midterms, its price went over a cliff, plummeting from just under $6 to a record low of $5.05. The internet noticed and offered its thoughts on the matter.
“Trump Media stock is down,” Washington Post contributor Drew Harwell pointed out . “A share costs about as much as a Happy Meal. At its peak, investors paid $175 a share.” But as writer Amanda Knox noted , “With a Happy Meal, you get a toy that you can keep.”
“Do not buy the dip,” warned New Yorker staff writer Philip Gourevitch. “If you're baffled by Trump voters, consider Trump investors,” mused another comment.
“Chugging this stuff until my torso kerplodes,” admitted one reshare of the disastrous stock chart. And All In producer Adam Weinstein needed no words to express his sentiments, adding only a clip from Mad Men in which character Don Draper achieves a moment of zen.
This isn’t the first time Trump’s company has been hit by bad financial news. In 2025, Truth Social reported net losses of $712 million. At the same time, data suggests that its traffic has fallen by 30 percent year over year, while its users dropped from a peak of roughly 420,000 in June 2025 to about 260,000 in September 2026. In 2023, it was also reported that TMTG was under investigation for laundering money for Russian oligarchs. While TMTG sued the Guardian and Variety for reporting on the story, the suit was dismissed. According to the Washington Post, a federal probe found that one of the company’s wealthy investors was linked to efforts to move assets from Russia, Ukraine, and China to the Caribbean. Over the past two years, the company has been increasingly involved with various cryptocurrency ventures, and the Trump family ’s crypto schemes have reportedly raked in roughly $2.3 billion since he reentered the White House.

Homebuilders and housing supplier stocks jumped on Wednesday in the wake of the midterm elections.

The 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ), the benchmark for mortgage rates, moved slightly lower.
The Democrats' sweep in Congress is fueling anticipation of new action in Washington on housing affordability, a prominent issue during the midterm campaign, and the potential for lower mortgage rates in a shifting macroeconomic environment.
The housing market is mired in an unyielding rut, hemmed in by high home prices and high mortgage rates. Homebuyers, especially younger, first-time buyers, are struggling to break into the market.

Despite the deadlock, Congress passed the first major piece of housing legislation in decades this year, a sprawling bill that addresses housing affordability by encouraging more homebuilding, expanding financing options, providing grants for local governments that ease zoning restrictions and expand the housing supply, and streamlining environmental review processes, among other provisions.
With Democrats assuming power and promising to address Americans' cost-of-living concerns, more legislative action could materialize — particularly on the demand side.
TD Cowen wrote in a post-election note that Rep. Maxine Waters of California, who could become chair of the House Financial Services Committee, plans to focus on housing, including down payment help and funds to renovate public housing. The analysts added, however, that they "remain dubious it will become law."

articles.title_orig: Unofficial AUKUS inquiry recommends tearing up the 'worst' defense decision the country has ever made
articles.title_zh: Unofficial AUKUS inquiry recommends tearing up the 'worst' defense decision the country has ever made
articles.content_orig:
Australia has agreed to take responsibility for highly radioactive nuclear waste from its AUKUS submarines without publicly naming where it will be disposed of, an arrangement inquiry lead commissioner Peter Garrett has labelled “astonishing, reckless and cavalier”.
This article is licensed under Creative Commons — Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International (CC BY-ND 4.0) .
Australia has agreed to take responsibility for highly radioactive nuclear waste from its AUKUS submarines without publicly naming where it will be disposed of, an arrangement inquiry lead commissioner Peter Garrett has labelled “astonishing, reckless and cavalier”.
Speaking at the National Press Club (NPC), the former Labor minister raised concerns about Australia’s ability to deal with the waste as he outlined the findings of an independent five-month inquiry that has called for the submarine deal to be scrapped and a royal commission established.
Mr Garrett questioned why Australia was pressing ahead when “after 60 years, and with more money and nuclear expertise than Australia, neither the UK nor the US has managed to develop and construct a permanent below ground high level radioactive waste storage facility”.
“Yet somehow, that same massive infrastructure challenge, with its attendant risk management requirements, is expected to materialise here overnight,” he said.
In September, Defence Minister Richard Marles said Australia would need to establish a dedicated disposal facility , but the first spent submarine reactors would not require disposal until the early 2050s.
He said it would be located on existing or future Defence land that is geologically stable and away from populations.
“We’re starting the process of thinking about how we go to the determination of a site,” he said.
Mr Garrett argued the uncertainty was particularly concerning for First Nations communities, given Australia’s history of nuclear testing and proposals to store radioactive waste on Indigenous land.
Quality research, analysis, explainers and factchecks from experts you can trust.
“For First Peoples, with a history of suffering the impact of nuclear testing, and whose lands, often in remote locations, are constantly put forward as the most suitable place to bury toxic material that lasts thousands of years, this omission is galling.”
Former Australian Defence Force chief and fellow commissioner Chris Barrie warned that Australia’s obligations extended to highly enriched uranium in the submarine reactors, with no publicly identified permanent disposal site.
He pointed to a controversial proposal to establish an international nuclear waste repository in South Australia a decade ago, which was abandoned after failing to win community support .
“That is salutary. Any plan to dispose of highly enriched uranium waste in Australia will be unacceptable to many Australians,” he said.
The inquiry has called for the nuclear-powered submarine deal to be scrapped immediately, and a royal commission be established.
“I have fewer years ahead of me than those left behind. Younger Australians will live with these choices far longer than I will,” said Retired Admiral Barrie.
“We owe them more than assurances. We owe them an honest account of the dangers, the alternatives, and the decisions being made in their name.”
