articles.title_orig: Oil tumbles below $100 on post-election peace hopes
articles.title_zh: Oil tumbles below $100 on post-election peace hopes
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices tumbled Wednesday after Vice President JD Vance blamed the war against Iran for Republican midterm election reversals.
U.S. West Texas Intermediate lost 8.3% to close at $88.12 a barrel. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, shed 8.7% to settle at $94.62.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance said in a social media post Wednesday. "The president himself said so last night."
Democrats swept the House and Senate in Tuesday's elections, giving the party leverage to pressure President Donald Trump to end the unpopular war that has spiked gasoline and diesel prices.
"The elections are leading the market to conclude that Trump might now be inclined to make a deal," said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates.
The Democrats may try to restrict funding for the war, Lipow said. Trump's announcement earlier this week that the U.S. will cut some funding to Israel could force Jerusalem to accept Washington's decisions, he said.
Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that he has no immediate plans to strike Iran. The oil market had priced in the risk of a major escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October.
Oil futures have fallen more than 14% this week as senior U.S. and Iranian officials indicated they're open to a diplomatic settlement of the conflict, which has disrupted global energy supplies for eight months.
The sell-off "could be getting a bit overdone," said Rebecca Babin, senior energy trader at CIBC. The market is in a "shoot first, ask questions" later mode as emotions run high after the unexpected election results, Babin said.
Many observers expected a Democrat tsunami could push Trump to escalate with Iran, Babin said. "Vance's commentary and the public lack of backing from key allies have challenged that assumption," she said.
But the odds still favor military escalation in the region, warned Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy and a former advisor to President George W. Bush.
"Iran is hardened in its uncompromising position," McNally said. "Trump, having now paid a huge price for his determination to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, is unlikely to let go of this legacy goal and walk away."

Developer Santa Monica Studio has just announced its upcoming game, God of War Laufey , has been delayed.
Originally planned for release on 16th February 2027, the PS5 exclusive action game will now launch just over three months later on 20th May.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen," the statement says. "We don't take for granted the trust placed in our studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans."
Santa Monica Studio says it'll "make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential."
God of War Laufey is the next entry in Sony's popular action series, chronicling the journey of Kratos' late wife, Faye, as she navigates the afterlife.
As mentioned in the above statement, the game was officially announced in June of this year, and even then it appeared to be close to release. At the time, some thought Sony was pushing Laufey harder than the imminent Marvel's Wolverine .
Still, the game will launch within a year of its announcement, which is pretty good going.

articles.title_orig: AI data-center stocks slide, renewables rally after Democratic US midterm sweep
articles.title_zh: AI data-center stocks slide, renewables rally after Democratic US midterm sweep
articles.content_orig:
Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress and securing historic wins in traditionally conservative states, as voters delivered a setback to President Donald Trump.
The party was projected to gain control of both chambers of Congress, with victories across several battleground states threatening to constrain Trump's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his presidency.
Here are some of the scenes from polling stations, campaign headquarters and election-night celebrations across the United States.
Among the biggest surprises was Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the state's first Democratic U.S. senator since 1988.
Fellow Democrat Gina Hinojosa also unseated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the state's first Latina governor and ending more than three decades of Republican control of the office.
In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a Republican-held Senate seat after defeating Trump-backed Michael Whatley. Cooper will succeed retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his departure after clashing with Trump over his tax and spending legislation.
In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Mike Collins, while former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state.
Meanwhile, in Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback, defeating Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a closely watched Senate race.
The elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's second term, with concerns over the cost of living, inflation and the war in Iran weighing on voter sentiment.
—CNBC's Danielle DeVries contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: Big Tech Stocks Soar as Traders Bet Democrats Will Slow AI Spend
articles.title_zh: Big Tech Stocks Soar as Traders Bet Democrats Will Slow AI Spend
articles.content_orig:
Democrats decisively took control of Congress Tuesday night, delivering a stinging rebuke to President Donald Trump and his economic record as voters voiced deep frustration with rising prices, government corruption and the AI data center build-out .
The party scored an extraordinary pair of victories in traditionally Republican Texas. James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the state in nearly four decades. Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Gov. Greg Abbott, making her the first Democratic governor of Texas since Ann Richards left office in 1995. Texas became the clearest measure of how far the blue wave reached: Democrats swept the state's marquee races in a Republican stronghold long considered beyond their grasp.
Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results
The victories were part of a broader wave of Democratic gains. In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews upset Darline Graham in a race Republicans had expected to win. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Democrats also flipped Senate seats in Iowa and North Carolina and won key races in Georgia and New Hampshire.
The results marked a striking collapse for Trump's candidates. Paxton, Graham and Husted were among the president's prominent picks who lost after he made dozens of endorsements.
The election also sharpened the political fight over data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure . Texas is a major center of planned data-center construction , and Hinojosa campaigned for a pause on new projects until the state adopts tougher rules. Her victory gives Democrats more influence over Texas' approach to the build-out, though the state Legislature remains in Republican hands.
The results also delivered a blow to the tech billionaires and corporate interest groups that poured hundreds of millions of dollars into backing Republican candidates who might be friendly to the massive AI data center projects they hope to build around the country. Elon Musk, the world's richest man and the cycle's largest individual political donor, spent record sums in a failed effort to help Republicans retain power, including in Texas.
Musk's spending may have become a liability as voters raised concerns about government corruption and the growing influence of billionaires in exit polls. Talarico repeatedly attacked Musk on the campaign trail, accusing him of trying to buy "his very own personal United States Senator."
"Tonight's results are a wake-up call for corporate special interests and billionaires who have been rigging the economy," said Rep. Chris Pappas, who defeated former Republican Sen. John Sununu to win an open Senate seat in New Hampshire.
The outcome is poised to reshape the technology sector's relationship with Washington. A more adversarial Congress is likely to intensify scrutiny of tech companies and the AI data center build-out. Markets reacted as the scale of Democratic gains became clear: Dow futures fell and S&P 500 futures slipped Tuesday evening.
Economic frustration was also central to Democratic gains. Many voters blamed Trump's tariffs and the war with Iran for worsening their economic situation, while the cost of living remained a persistent strain.
Democratic control of both chambers gives the party a powerful check on Trump in the final two years of his term, including the ability to block parts of his agenda and intensify congressional oversight. The results sent a clear warning: promises to bring down costs did not overcome voters' frustration with prices, corruption and the country's direction.
Silicon Valley spent record sums trying to shape the election. Instead, it got a Democratic House promising to haul its CEOs before congressional investigators.
Many of the winners ran against not just Trump, but the billionaire donors who helped bankroll Republicans. In North Carolina, Cooper told supporters that North Carolinians "will always matter more than the billionaires and the insiders."
In Texas, Talarico defeated Paxton despite more than $200 million from SpaceX CEO Musk to stop him. On the same ballot, Hinojosa defeated Abbott after blaming him for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, saying the governor for putting Big Tech interests ahead of local communities.
The GOP had a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans exclusively or nearly so. Crypto, AI, and online gambling interests poured more than $377 million into races.
Not all of Silicon Valley's money ended up on the losing side. LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, one of Democrats' biggest donors, cast the results as "an overwhelming wave against Trump and his cronies" and took a direct shot at Musk.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote on X late Tuesday. "And while people like Elon are spending outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power, those of us who believe in the ideals of America cannot yield."
With control of the House comes the power to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and examine the Trump administration and its allies. That's going to be a challenge for tech companies to navigate as they find themselves in Democratic crosshairs.
Democrats are already calling for AI executives to testify under oath.
Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
"The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath."
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the presumptive next chair of the oversight committee, put it more simply: "Lawyer up," he said in a statement.
The results also present headwinds for the infrastructure undergirding AI.
The Texas results appear to be a warning sign for the AI industry in a state projected to overtake Virginia as the world's biggest data center market by 2030, according to JLL . Abbott had long courted data center development before shifting his position this year as the backlash grew. Talarico and Hinojosa both seized on that anger, winning over Republican voters fed up with data centers going up in their communities. Hinojosa has promised to force lawmakers to regulate the industry .
In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans.
Trump personally pushed states to redistrict their congressional seats mid-decade to cement a Republican majority in the House. The effort largely flopped.
Many of the GOP's redrawn districts ended up falling to Democrats, despite the unprecedented effort to defend or flip them by redrawing boundaries mid-decade.
That includes seats in Texas, Florida and North Carolina, which Democrats won despite Republicans making them safer. In Texas, where Republicans began their redistricting war that then spread to other states, Democrats ended up winning most of the gerrymandered seats.
The redistricting push was always risky because no recent census was available when the maps were drawn.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Paxton, only for Republicans to lose a Senate seat in Texas for the first time in over three decades.
Talarico's victory in Texas came after Trump endorsed Paxton over the incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who held the seat for decades. In endorsing Paxton, Trump said Cornyn had not been sufficiently loyal.
Paxton prevailed in a bitter primary, and Trump's move to tip the scales spurned Senate Republicans, who saw Cornyn as a better and less expensive candidate than Paxton — who had a laundry list of scandals that plagued his campaign.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Starship Will Need To Re-Fuel 22 Times In Space To Make It To The Moon
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Starship Will Need To Re-Fuel 22 Times In Space To Make It To The Moon
articles.content_orig:
Nobody outside SpaceX and NASA can say today how many Starship launches it will take to put American astronauts on the Moon. Space, Mjengo Hub and 9to5Google all frame the launch count as an open question, and the refueling plan behind it as anything but simple. NASA selected SpaceX to build the Starship Human Landing System (HLS) for Artemis, and the agency’s own architecture depends on tanker Starships filling an orbital storage vehicle before the lander departs Earth orbit.
That gap between a clear concept and a missing number matters for hardware watchers. Every extra tanker flight means more Super Heavy boosters, more Raptor engines and more pad turnarounds. The count drives cost, schedule and risk, so a loose estimate of six launches versus forty is the difference between a stretch goal and a different program.
Meanwhile the physical pieces of the other half of the mission keep moving. Our report on the Artemis III core stage joining its boosters in the Vehicle Assembly Building shows the NASA side of the stack taking shape while the SpaceX side still lacks a published launch tally.
Don't miss new tech stories on Google
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.
Start with the solid ground. NASA selected SpaceX to develop the Starship HLS for the Artemis program, and the vehicle is meant to carry astronauts between lunar orbit and the Moon’s surface. That is the confirmed core, and it comes straight from NASA’s description of the program.
The architecture NASA describes includes an orbital propellant storage Starship that tanker Starships supply. The human-rated Starship is planned to launch to that storage vehicle in Earth orbit, refuel, and continue on toward lunar orbit. In other words, the lander does not leave Earth with a full tank. It tops off in orbit first.
SpaceX adds a payload claim to this picture. The company states that on-orbit refilling can let Starship deliver up to 100 tons directly to the lunar surface. That figure is SpaceX’s own and describes capability, not a schedule or a launch count.
Crew transport stays with NASA hardware. Artemis astronauts launch aboard Orion on the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket, and NASA’s stated plan has Orion rendezvous and dock with Starship HLS in Earth orbit before the combined vehicle heads toward the Moon. So two very different launch systems must meet in space for the mission to work.
Finally, NASA and SpaceX have both publicly described an orbital refueling demonstration involving a depot and tanker Starships. What neither has published, according to the sources reviewed for this story, is a binding number of tanker flights. That omission is the whole story.
Starship’s design philosophy rests on reuse and volume. The Super Heavy booster launches the ship from Earth, runs on Raptor engines and is designed to be fully reusable. That approach buys enormous lift for a low cost per flight, but it does not stretch to a fully fueled lunar lander in a single go.
The reason is simple physics. A vehicle that reaches Earth orbit has already spent a large share of its propellant getting there. To send a heavy lander on to the Moon, land, and return crew to lunar orbit, it needs far more fuel than remains after the climb. Refueling in orbit solves that by splitting the delivery across several launches.
This is why the plan hinges on a storage vehicle and tankers. The storage Starship acts as a parking lot for propellant. Tankers fly up, transfer their loads, and return. Once enough has accumulated, the human-rated Starship arrives, fills up, and departs.
The catch sits in the word “enough.” How much propellant the lander needs, how much each tanker can usefully deliver after losses, and how much evaporates while waiting all feed the launch count. None of those inputs appears in the official sources as a final figure. That is why every precise tally floating around online deserves skepticism.
Compare that with the payload economics we covered in the 26-satellite Starship flight and its $715M upside . Commercial flights make money by flying often. A lunar campaign asks the same machine to fly often for a single mission, which is a different kind of stress test.
The refueling concept has several moving parts, and each one must work before the next matters. NASA and SpaceX describe the broad sequence, though not every detail or timing.
A propellant storage Starship goes to Earth orbit first. Tanker Starships follow, each carrying propellant to hand over. The storage vehicle collects those deliveries and holds them until the lander is ready to arrive.
Later, the human-rated Starship launches to the storage vehicle, takes on propellant and continues to lunar orbit. NASA’s description of the architecture treats this as the central trick of the whole mission. Everything about the lander’s size and ambition depends on it.
Crew do not ride Starship from the ground. They fly on Orion, carried by SLS, and NASA’s stated architecture has Orion dock with Starship HLS in Earth orbit. The combined vehicle then travels toward the Moon.
Orion has already shown it can survive a lunar return. Our coverage of Artemis II’s 252,756-mile record and the heat shield that held covers that hardware story. The docking handoff with a refueled Starship is the next piece NASA still has to prove.
Several numbers circulate in coverage of this topic. Sorting them by what an official source supports shows how thin the confirmed list is. The table below separates the solid facts from the secondary-reporting figures.
Notice what lands in the confirmed rows. They describe the shape of the plan, not its size. Every row that carries a launch count falls into the unconfirmed bucket.
The most quoted estimate is a range of six to eight launches. Secondary reporting attributes it to Elon Musk, but the research behind this article could not trace it to an official NASA or SpaceX requirement. Treat it as a founder’s estimate, not a contract term.
That distinction is not pedantry. Executives often offer optimistic launch-count figures when describing a design goal. Official requirements, by contrast, appear in agreements and mission plans that name margins and failure cases. The six-to-eight number has the first character and none of the second.
Also, a low estimate and a high estimate can both be honest. If tankers improve, if boil-off turns out small and if transfer works on the first try, a low count becomes plausible. If any of those slip, the number climbs. Without published test data, outsiders cannot pick a side.
One earlier expert estimate put the campaign at 10 to 40 launches. The returned source describes it as an estimate from before the plan matured, and it does not set a requirement. A spread that wide mostly tells you how much depends on unproven transfer performance.
Some secondary reporting goes further than a raw count. It describes a requirement for more than 10 tanker flights, a cadence of roughly one launch every six days, and a refueling campaign that begins more than 200 days before the crew launches. None of these figures appears in the official NASA or SpaceX sources returned for this story.
Cadence matters because propellant does not wait politely. Cryogenic fuel warms and evaporates, so a long gap between tanker flights can undo earlier deliveries. A tight cadence reduces that loss, while a long campaign raises it. That tradeoff links the launch count directly to how fast SpaceX can turn a pad around.
SpaceX also flies its other programs from the same industrial base. The company’s schedule for the month is laid out in our November launch calendar with four Falcon 9 dates and one Starship flight . A lunar tanker campaign would have to share boosters, crews and pads with that wider manifest.
So the honest reading is this. A frequent-flight campaign is the logical consequence of the architecture, and the specific cadence numbers in circulation remain unverified. If you see a prec

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's leader says Russian "insane attack" on aid center may have killed 70 people, pleads for air defenses
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's leader says Russian "insane attack" on aid center may have killed 70 people, pleads for air defenses
articles.content_orig:
School in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region was struck on Monday
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy – fresh back from his meetings in Germany yesterday and today – has offered an update on the search and rescue operations after the Russian strike on a school in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region on Monday.
40 people have been confirmed dead, with fears that more than 30 may still be under the rubble, Zelenskyy said.
“ Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack. But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response. Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered.”
And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today .
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that 40 people were confirmed dead and more than 30 missing after “insane” Russian attack on a school in Ukraine on Monday ( 14:44 ), just days before key trilateral peace talks with the US and Russia.
Zelenskyy continues his trip of Europe and after visiting Germany where he was hosted by chancellor Friedrich Merz, he is now expected in Spain.
His comments came as the EU hosted key technical talks with the US, some EU countries, Nato, and the World Bank on Ukraine ( 10:05 ).
Following the US midterm elections, some European leaders expressed hopes that the result will put Donald Trump under pressure to make progress in talks with Moscow and Kyiv ( 12:18 , 12:57 , 14:31 ).
But some leaders also expressed concerns about the political consequences of the vote ( 11:31 , 11:55 , 12:45 ).
Montenegro could be in a position to join the European Union as early as 2028 with accession negotiations concluded by the end of this year, after the bloc praised the country for advancing “the reforms needed” to complete the process ( 13:33 ).
If you are after more reactions to the US midterm elections, you can follow our US live blog here:
If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.
I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has landed in Spain, where he is expected to take part in talks with key leaders from Spain and Latin America, as well as the UN secretary-general and the European Council president, according to Spain’s El País newspaper.
The paper reported that Zelenskyy will take part in “several high-level meetings” on the sidelines of the Ibero-American summit in Madrid, hosted by Spain’s embattled prime minister Pedro Sánchez.
Argetina’s controversial president Javier Milei is believed to be among the guests. Portugal will be represented by PM Luís Montenegro .
Just like in Berlin, Zelenskyy’s trip was kept secret until his plane touched down for security reasons, El País said.
In other news, France’s national blood service has said hackers accessed control systems and boosted temperatures at three cold stores stocking vital blood products , in an apparent escalation of recent cyber-attacks on fridges and freezers across Europe.
The French blood service (EFS) said temperature and defrosting thresholds had been raised to “very high levels” in the attack , adding that its alarm systems had allowed technicians to intervene before the products were compromised.
The EFS is France’s public blood transfusion operator, collecting, testing, preparing and distributing products such as blood, plasma and platelets to more than 1,900 hospitals around the country. It supports more than a million patients a year.
The attack, which EFS said had occurred overnight on Monday, came as the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in supermarkets in almost a dozen European countries soared as high as 50C (122F), causing millions of euros of food damage.
Here is some more on how Italy’s far-right prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who once had good relations with Donald Trump, dismissed questions about the midterm election results, telling journalists “let’s talk about America another time”.
Meloni, wearing a red suit, had been door-stepped while attending a ceremony in central Rome on Wednesday to mark Italy’s national unity and armed forces day and didn’t welcome the journalistic focus on the US midterms.
“I see you’re very interested in the celebration of the republic and the Armed Forces,” she said sarcastically.
Meloni had positioned herself as a key European ally to Trump until April, when the pair fell out, firstly over Italy’s refusal to support the US-Israeli war in Italy and then because of Trump’s extraordinary broadside against Pope Leo in reaction to the pontiff’s condemnation of the war.
They had appeared to be getting relations back on track at the G7 summit in June before Trump claimed Meloni had begged him to take a photo with him - a story Meloni said was a “a total invention”.
Italy’s foreign minister Antonio Tajani did instead comment on the midterms, saying Italy’s relationship with the US “remains unchanged regardless of who is in government or the parliamentary situation”.
In an interview with the Rome-based newspaper, Il Messaggero, Tajani said “we have never been Trumpians” and “Meloni isn’t a Maga supporter either – heaven forbid!”
The League, which is led by joint deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini, who until fairly recently continuously praised Trump, said in a statement:
“When a population votes, their vote must always be respected and understood.”
The party also expressed hope that the outcome would speed-up efforts to end wars and restore peace.
European Union ⁠foreign policy ⁠chief Kaja ​Kallas said ⁠on Wednesday that “US ⁠voters ​have made ‌their ‌choice clear”, ‌commenting on the country’s midterms election results.
She ‌said she hoped ​Congress would continue ⁠to support Ukraine ​and put ​more ​pressure ​on ‌Russia.
“I hope that the new Congress... will continue supporting Ukraine and also putting more pressure on Russia ,” Kallas said, adding that Europe and the United States “are much stronger together” in pushing Moscow to end its war.
The European Union has offered fresh hope for Serbia’s membership talks if the election-winning student movement there forms a government willing to strengthen democracy.
The election of a diverse student-led opposition movement could provide an opening for a reset with the most influential of the western Balkan countries in line at Europe’s door, AP reported.
“ Now Serbia has the chance for a fresh start ,” enlargement commissioner Marta Kos told EU lawmakers as she debriefed them on the report.
“The new Serbian government has an opportunity to turn the page, strengthen democratic institutions and fundamental rights and take the necessary steps to advance on Serbia’s accession path ,” she added.
Serbia could progress rapidly under a government with strong political will but membership currently looks years away.
It comes as the the European Commission said in its enlargement report that Montenegro is on track to become the EU’s 28th member in 2028 ( see post 12.33 ) - and that Albania and Moldova could join the following year.
However, Ukraine is unlikely to meet the conditions for joining before the end of the decade.

articles.title_orig: UK national tests positive for Ebola virus in DR Congo
articles.title_zh: UK national tests positive for Ebola virus in DR Congo
articles.content_orig:
A British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo will be flown back to the UK.
It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.
It is not clear when the flight will take place.
Earlier, a UK government spokesperson said there were "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and that the risk to the public remains low.
Reuters news agency reported the infected man is a healthcare worker, citing an internal document BBC News has not seen.
Imported Ebola cases are extremely rare in the UK and have resulted in no deaths.
There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK - one, in 1976, resulting from a laboratory incident, and three involving health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.
A UK government spokesperson said: "The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated.
"Further information will be shared in due course as appropriate. The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low."
There have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the recent outbreak in DR Congo started in May, which has grown to become the second most deadly recorded spate of infections, behind the outbreak in West Africa.
It has since become the deadliest in the country's history, with a fatality rate of 48.6% reported at the end of last month.
Ebola can result in serious illness and death. Early symptoms include vomiting and diarrhoea but it can progress to organ failure and internal bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The ongoing outbreak centred on DR Congo is fueled by the Bundibugyo variant of the virus.
There is no approved vaccine but the World Health Organisation said experts have recommended adding two new candidate drugs to an ongoing clinical trial.
The vaccines, one developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and another by the firm Moderna, will join the trial once they are approved by Congolese health authorities.
It will be the first time jabs specifically designed to protect against the Bundibugyo virus are tested during an outbreak.
Since the outbreak, Ebola cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
Additional reporting by Richard Kagoe

articles.title_orig: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling
articles.title_zh: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling
articles.content_orig:
Britta has been a technology journalist for 15 years, covering everything from phones, tablets and fitness devices, to smart home and beauty tech. Britta spent 10 years as deputy editor of technology site Pocket-lint. Now freelance, she is co-founder of reviews website The Disconnekt and writes for various publications including The Telegraph, British GQ, Metro and Good Housekeeping. Britta has also been a guest on a number of radio stations, including BBC Radio, Siren FM and Academy FM, as well as the Big Tech Show Podcast.
The products or services listed have been independently tested by our journalists. We earn a commission from the affiliate links in this article. Read more >
Amazon and Google have had the kitchen worktop to themselves for most of the last decade with the Echo Show and Nest Hub devices. Now Apple has joined the fray with the £299 HomeView, which works with its newly AI-powered Siri virtual assistant.
I was at the New York launch to get a first look at Apple’s entry into the “smart display” market. These smart speakers with tablet-like touchscreens and integrated cameras do everything from playing music and displaying recipes to video calls and showing you who is at the front door via a video doorbell .
The Homeview’s seven-inch square screen handles all the above – assuming you have compatible devices – and for me, most interestingly, its built-in camera recognises registered users and adapts the display accordingly for up to six household members with their own messages, calendars and reminders.
But how else does it challenge rivals’ capabilities and will it appeal to non-iPhone users?
HomeView stands out with its square display and domed aluminium speaker base. The Echo Show and Nest Hub have rectangular screens with fabric-covered bases, great for watching TV while cooking but terrible for worktop spills.
There are two HomeView models, table-top and wall-mounted (I’d expect the table-top to be more popular on bedside tables and kitchen worktops). Surprisingly, neither has a visible Apple logo or physical buttons; you control volume and brightness on screen or via the Apple Home app on an iPhone or iPad.
It comes in four tasteful metallic shades that blend into the home, and screen faces that will feel familiar to anyone who uses an Apple device, especially an Apple Watch . You can customise each face with a range of colours and fonts, and swipe between them easily.
HomeView claims to instantly recognise a registered user in the built-in camera’s view and displays their home screen, apps and widgets when they swipe up from the bottom. When another user steps into frame, a prompt asks whether you want to switch profiles. If the first user leaves the camera’s view, their personal content disappears. There’s also a guest mode for non-registered users
Amazon and Google displays have used face and voice recognition for years to tailor parts of the experience, such as calendars, but Apple’s version is more comprehensive, reaching as far as your messages.
Smart displays have several advantages over smart speakers, but they shine in the kitchen because they can show recipes and cooking instructions. HomeView is particularly good here. Find a dish you want to cook in Safari on HomeView, or on your iPhone, and it will split the recipe into an ingredients list and a method that you swipe through step by step. Any times mentioned are highlighted in orange; tap one to start a timer. It’s smart, intuitive, and far better than on rival displays.
Most smart displays live or die by their voice assistants. Google’s Nest Hub uses Gemini, and Amazon’s Echo Show runs Alexa. HomeView uses Apple’s rebuilt assistant, Siri AI, which arrived on iPhones, iPads, Macs and Apple Watch with September’s software update.
It is a marked improvement on old Siri when paired with an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone or iPad (available on newer devices, including iPhone 16 or later and some iPhone 15 models). It can draw on personal context, such as your messages and calendar, to answer questions about your day. You can ask follow-up questions, play music, find lost devices , and ask general-knowledge questions that old Siri would have punted to a web search. It worked well in my demos.
Apple says it doesn’t store requests or make them accessible, and its privacy record is good so far. But an always-listening microphone, a face-scanning camera and an assistant that reads your messages are a lot to invite into the kitchen. Unlike the Echo Show and Nest Hub Max, there’s no physical switch to mute the microphone or disable the camera, either, though you can turn them all off in the settings if you wish.
HomeView can control smart lights, heating, security cameras and video doorbells via touch or voice, but devices must support Matter – the cross-brand smart home standard. That means you aren’t confined to Apple-approved gadgets, but you are still limited – Ring video doorbells, for example, aren’t Matter-compatible, so they won’t work with HomeView, which could be a deal-breaker for even the biggest Apple fan.
But for anyone put off by the complexity of setting up a smart home, Apple is trying to simplify things. It has partnered with LG on Home Collection – a range of devices, including security cameras and a video doorbell – that connect with a single tap, just as AirPods do with an iPhone. They won’t be available until later in the year, but they could mark a major step towards making smart home set-up less complicated.
HomeView is built for the Apple faithful: set-up requires an iPhone or iPad, personalised AI features need a recent Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone, and some apps work only when your phone is nearby. In a household split between iPhone and Android , Android users will get a much thinner experience, and Apple’s own services come first at every turn.
Still, HomeView is the most polished smart display I have seen. Face recognition makes it both a great shared and personalised device; the sound quality is excellent; and Siri AI is finally worth talking to, especially when it can draw on your personal context. I’ll need to live with it for a few weeks before giving a final verdict, but so far it’s a beautifully designed device I’d be happy to invite into my home.
HomeView is available to pre-order now, with availability from Nov 13, 2026. A wall-mounted version costs the same, with mounts sold separately. It won’t be sold in the EU at all, because Siri AI isn’t yet available there.
Apple HomeView costs £299 for both models. The mounts for the wall-mounted model start at £59.95, with three options. The most expensive option is £129.95.
The Apple HomeView tabletop model comes in four colours: a darker Space Grey, Silver, Rose Pink, and Starlight (a metallic gold). The wall-mounted model comes in Space Grey and Silver.

articles.title_orig: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.title_zh: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.content_orig:
The 2026 midterm elections delivered shocking wins for Democrats on Tuesday evening, reshaping the balance of power in Washington.
Business leaders, tech executives, and investors are now assessing what the new political landscape could mean for their industries as Democratic candidates flipped key Senate and House seats.
This includes Texas, where James Talarico won his Senate race despite over $150 million in funding from Elon Musk for his Republican rival, Ken Paxton.
After the results, some of the tech and business leaders who sought closer ties with President Donald Trump ahead of his return to the White House could face new congressional scrutiny.
In California, the results of the nation's first-ever ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with net worth exceeding $1 billion could have major implications for the state's elite, though as of around 7 a.m. ET, the "No" vote held a strong lead.
Here's how powerbrokers in business and tech reacted to the midterms results amid the blue wave sweeping across the country:
Reid Hoffman , the cofounder of LinkedIn and a Democratic megadonor, reacted to the party's big wins in a post on X Tuesday evening.
"Voters made clear they demand a different kind of country. Americans want an economy that can compete globally and deliver for them at home. And they made clear that they want leaders they can trust to fight for their constituents," he wrote.
"This night blew the doors off our expectations. From Texas to Ohio, Kentucky to Iowa, and South Carolina to Indiana, voters rejected the status quo. Tonight's lesson: Never discount any voter in any place," he continued.
Hoffman has been active in politics and vocal about his support for Democrats, spending tens of millions this election cycle. He also spent millions to support Kamala Harris's campaign in 2024.
Hoffman has previously said the Democratic Party had alienated Silicon Valley and was partly to blame for its shift to the right.
Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions to support Republicans, broke his silence late on election night with two short X posts.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said, referencing concerns that Democratic wins could mean more scrutiny on data center development.
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," he joked in a quick follow-up post.
Musk, the world's richest person, spent more money than any other individual in the midterms, donating a whopping $446 million, mostly in Texas, the state he calls home along with his companies Tesla and SpaceX.
In addition to Talarico's Senate seat, the Texas governorship was also won by a Democrat, Gina Hinojosa. It was the first time in decades a Democrat won a statewide race in the Lone Star state.
Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, saw the election results as showing that tech companies need to do more to convince people about the benefits of AI.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," she said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."
"I do think this is an opportunity for us as a tech industry to realize that we need to make sure that the value proposition is clear to every local community that is going to host a data center, and I believe we can do that," she added.
Dara Khosrowshahi , the CEO of Uber, shared his thoughts on the midterms in a Wednesday morning interview with CNBC.
"I think the people of our country sent a message regarding change," he said. "I think that continuous inflation really has taken a mark on the consumer."
"I think it's up to businesses and up to our politicians and leaders in Washington to respond, and I hope that they do, because it was a very clear message that was sent out."
Khorowshahi, who is Iranian by birth, was a vocal critic of Trump during his first term, but donated $1 million to the president's inaugural fund after the 2024 election.
Keith Rabois held executive roles at PayPal, LinkedIn, and Square, before becoming managing director at Khosla Ventures. As the results came in overnight, he posted on X: "Another reason to move to Miami."
It came shortly after the Associated Press called Florida's US Senate race for the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, who held on despite a strong Democratic swing.
While two of the city's three main congressional districts elected Democrats in huge swings, the one that covers downtown Miami looks set to narrowly reelect the Republican incumbent, with 99% of the vote counted.
Rabois is married to Jacob Helberg, Trump's undersecretary of state for economic affairs, and their wedding ceremony was officiated by Sam Altman.
Last year, The Wall Street Journal reported the couple was selling their Miami Beach home for $65 million as Helberg relocated to Washington, DC, although Rabois planned to stay based in Miami.
Brad Gerstner , CEO of Altimeter Capital, had thoughts on how the US data center buildout would be affected by the elections.
In a guest appearance on the All-In podcast livestream Tuesday evening, Gerstner said fears that a "blue tsunami" could make it difficult to build new data centers are "overblown."
But he said that election results could slow down the development of the centers, and candidates like Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who won the Texas gubernatorial race Tuesday, could "issue a moratorium on new data centers." He said this could be "really challenging for the AI infratrade."
Gerstner also said that Republicans and the AI community have "struggled with the messaging" over AI as the affordability crisis has weighed on Americans' minds.
The investor is the architect of "Trump Accounts," the investment vehicle for children in the country that launched in July.
Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, hinted at what he believes a blue wave could mean for the AI buildout.
"I am now bullish space datacenters," Patel said in a post on X alongside a screenshot of results out of Texas that showed Hinojosa with an early lead over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
Ahead of the midterms, some in tech expressed concern that Democratic wins would mean additional scrutiny on data centers, which have faced fierce opposition in communities across the US.
Dan Ives, a veteran Wall Street analyst and AI bull, said the midterms will put the brakes on the rapid construction of data centers.
In a post on X, he said the "Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years."
Ives added that while some investors will prefer a slower pace, others will view it as added risk.
"We estimate 10% of data centers will not happen now," he said.
Richard Branson, the billionaire founder of the Virgin Group, wrote in a post on LinkedIn that the results of the midterm election are not just "a decisive repudiation of Trump" but also an encouraging sign "about the limits of money in politics."
Branson wrote, "As a successful entrepreneur, I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent on — mostly Republican — campaigns this election cycle, in an attempt to buy influence and control over public policy."
Branson added that voters looked past the "hateful and false messages" fueled by the billions spent on funding candidates, voting based on the issues that mattered to them.
"I hope this will prompt the next Congress to start a fresh conversation about the toxic impact of money in politics and the need for meaningful campaign finance reform," he wrote.

articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in

Outback Steakhouse’s largest U.S. franchisee has filed for bankruptcy , putting 61 western restaurants up for sale as the chain’s parent company seeks to take them over.
Out West Restaurant Group, also known as Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy Monday after years of declining sales and rising costs. Its financial troubles date back to 2018, when falling restaurant traffic began eating into revenue. The pandemic further deepened the losses, with revenue plunging 35 percent in 2020, according to court filings .
The franchisee has reached a $26.3 million agreement with Outback’s parent company, Bloomin’ Brands, to sell its restaurants and assets. The deal serves as a “stalking horse” bid, establishing a minimum starting price that other potential buyers can attempt to beat during the bankruptcy process.
Bloomin’ Brands is providing up to $5.5 million to keep the restaurants open during bankruptcy with no immediate changes expected for customers or employees.
The steakhouse chain has around 115 franchised restaurants in the U.S., along with about 544 company-owned locations. If Bloomin’ Brands completes the acquisition, it would take direct control of more than half of Outback’s remaining U.S. franchised restaurants, according to Restaurant Dive .
Bloomin’ said it was “working closely with Out West, its lenders, and other stakeholders throughout the Bankruptcy Court-supervised process as it focuses on maintaining stability in Out West’s restaurant operations, supporting Team Members and continuing to serve guests,” Restaurant Dive reports.
The company said that buying Out West’s restaurants “gives [Bloomin’] direct operational insight, allows it to invest in the units through its development initiatives, and to mitigate disruption to guests and employees.”
Out West’s restaurants are primarily located in the Southwest with locations in Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico and Colorado. The company also has significant creditors in California, according to bankruptcy filings cited by Restaurant Dive .
News of the bankruptcy filing comes as Outback revamps its menu and kitchen practices to improve food quality and win back diners.
The changes include adding a New York strip to its regular menu for the first time and introducing a thick-cut ribeye called the “Down Under Delmonico.” Outback is also updating its cut specifications, hand-trimming techniques and seasoning methods for existing favorites, including its center-cut sirloin, Rockhampton ribeye and Victoria’s barrel-cut filet mignon, the company said.
Bloomin' Brands also owns Carrabba's Italian Grill, Bonefish Grill and Fleming's Prime Steakhouse & Wine Bar.

articles.title_orig: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
articles.title_zh: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The US midterm elections could have consequences far beyond the country’s borders. President Donald Trump has spent nearly two years overturning decades of American foreign policy, unsettling allies and adversaries alike. Now, both are watching to see how an electoral setback at home will shape his actions abroad.
For Iran, Israel and Ukraine, the stakes go well beyond who controls Congress. The result could influence whether Trump pursues a deal with Tehran or more war, how much Washington’s longstanding support for Israel erodes, and how hard he pushes Kyiv to accept terms to end Russia’s war.
Democrats will have new tools to challenge Trump. But he still has considerable freedom to act abroad, leaving world leaders with a question: Will defeat make him more willing to compromise, or more determined to get his way?
Here’s how the vote could impact Washington’s most pressing foreign policy concerns:
Iran is celebrating Trump’s midterm setback, but it is bracing for what comes next: a possible new US strike or a fresh push for a deal.
Trump admitted in a call with Fox News that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans’ losses but Vice President JD Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.”
After eight months of striking the region’s economic lifelines to turn American voters against the war, Tehran has hailed the Republican loss as a public verdict on it. Trump acknowledged that war-driven price hikes played a role.
“If the US government betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has led negotiations with the US, wrote on X.
Tehran is not betting on a change of course in Washington. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said anyone who believes the results will shift US policy is “deeply mistaken,” and officials say Iran’s strategy doesn’t hinge on American elections as they prepare for more war while intensifying diplomacy.
The risk of escalation is real. Reports that Trump might order new, more intense strikes are fueling anxiety across the region, and Tehran has warned that its retaliation would be much wider in scope than in earlier rounds. This week, Trump told some journalists he is considering striking Iran hard, and others that he has no immediate plans to escalate.
Top Republicans blame Iran war for midterm results
“The Iran war has become a political albatross around his neck, leaving (Trump) with a stark choice: cut a face-saving deal and declare victory, or double down militarily to reclaim the initiative,” Ali Vaez of International Crisis Group told CNN. “The danger is that a president weakened at the ballot box may seek redemption on the battlefield.”
Diplomacy offers another path. Talks that stagnated over the summer have picked up in the past week, with Tehran sending officials to Qatari mediators who are circulating proposals with Washington. Before the vote, Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Trump agreed to its seven conditions.
Sanam Vakil of Chatham House said Iran’s leadership “might feel vindicated,” but that “does not necessarily solve their problems.” Trump needs a diplomatic victory yet may be reluctant to appear weak, she said, while Tehran could read his setback as a chance to demand greater concessions. She expects intensified diplomacy alongside military threats, with an interim Strait of Hormuz deal “more realistic” than a comprehensive one.
In Israel, the election day announcement that Trump would abruptly cut off US military aid to the country was the first surprise. The results, with Democrats sweeping both chambers of Congress in what has been called a “blue tsunami,” are a five-alarm fire in Israel.
Bipartisan support for Israel in the US had already been eroding, with Democrats outraged at Israel over the death toll in the Gaza war and a growing number of Republicans believing the US has given it too much support.
“The only bipartisan issue right now is criticism of Israel,” said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to the US. “It’s an organizing principle for the Democratic Party,” he told CNN. “And it’s becoming an organizing principle for much of the Republican Party.”
Oren said the end of US aid is just the beginning of a process that has only started to play out. He said it’s conceivable that the US could end intelligence sharing with Israel and the joint development of critical military systems, such as the vaunted Iron Dome aerial defense system. He also pointed to the United Nations Security Council, where Republican and Democratic presidents have protected Israel with the US veto.
“We are at the end of an era,” he said.
Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift in US politics
Yaakov Katz, a former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, warned there is more to come. “What Trump announced about the military aid yesterday is just the tip of the iceberg of what can change – arms sales could be blocked, sanctions will be proposed and joint economic programs defunded,” he said on X.
The anti-Israel sentiment only hardened during the Iran war, with segments of the US electorate viewing the joint US-Israel strikes as a war that Netanyahu sold to Trump. Even now, Netanyahu has been pushing to resume strikes on Iran, which would reignite a war that drove gas prices and the cost of living higher and contributed to Republicans’ devastating midterm performance.
Netanyahu also faces turmoil at home. In elections a week before the midterms, he lost his majority in parliament, but his main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, does not have an outright majority and would likely need to cooperate with Arab parties, who saw record turnout.
Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, warned that Israel “does not have time to waste” in replacing Netanyahu and leading the country away from sanctions and isolation.
For Kyiv, the reaction came before the election. And on Wednesday there was relative silence.
For weeks, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s relationship with Trump has been in freefall. Trump has demanded Zelensky be replaced; courted energy deals to benefit Russia; and watched as Ukraine’s tech and intel dependencies on the US were inexplicably thwarted. And so Kyiv was forced to take a position early: wait, with urgency, for a post-Trump world.
And when it began to dawn on Wednesday, there was little official comment from Kyiv, Zelensky perhaps happy for the memes of him, sat with a beer and popcorn in front of the mid-term TV coverage, to do the job for him.
A deputy in his office, Sergiy Kyslytsia, pledged on Ukrainian TV that the country would continue to “develop genuine, normal and stable relations” with whoever is in office, seek Patriot interceptors, and navigate both a new Congress and the likely flurry of executive orders that may try to obviate it.
But there can be no disguising that a crestfallen Trump, and the slow clock now loudly ticking on his worldview and presidency, is in Kyiv’s favour. He had claimed a peace was easy to fashion, yet proceeded to punish Ukraine for not agreeing to the demands of its invader. He humiliated, scolded, and then occasionally made up with, Zelensky, while massaged by European allies, aghast at the breakdown in decades of security alliances.
There is still a lot that Ukraine needs Trump and the United States to do. Provide arms, money, and a wider assurance it is on their side. But Kyiv has calculated it cannot depend on Washington, after months of hostility.
There is one downside of the ticking clock however: that Russian President Vladimir Putin determines he has likely a year to pursue, at any cost, the best outcome possible in his war of choice, before the 2028 fight drags Republican policy back to the pro-Ukrainian mainstream. articles.title_orig: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
articles.title_zh: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
articles.content_orig:
Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange.
The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.
"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction."
He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.
Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker."
As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.
Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.
The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.
As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street."
"We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. "We're working around the clock with law enforcement agencies and with industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds for that front."

articles.title_orig: Data centers lost the midterms
articles.title_zh: Data centers lost the midterms
articles.content_orig:
Voters overwhelmingly rejected AI data centers on election night – dealing a major setback to Elon Musk and other tech bigwigs pushing a massive buildout.
At least 50 ballot measures dealing with data centers — either allowing them or limiting them — were up for consideration in states around the country. Voters decided against centers in 47 cases, with the outcome of three votes still pending as of Wednesday afternoon, according to data compiled by Ballotpedia .
The lone favorable outcome for the tech sector occurred in Harwood, ND, where local voters shot down a measure that would have imposed additional review requirements on industrial sites, including data centers, before they can move forward.
The biggest data center rebuke occurred in Ohio, where 21 ballot measures related to controversial sites were up for consideration. Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown focused heavily on the issue in his successful senatorial bid, painting Republican opponent Jon Husted as the “face of data centers.”
The nationwide rejection of data centers coincided with a “blue tsunami” for Democrats, who secured majorities in the House and Senate in a stunning rout.
Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who defeated longtime incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, has backed a moratorium on data center projects with an emphasis on making sure the facilities do not strain the power grid.
The outcome of the data center ballot initiatives could give members of the 120th Congress impetus to impose regulation on the sites, according to Ed Mills, a policy analyst for investment firm Raymond James.
“If they consistently see there’s an issue that voters support overwhelmingly, that is going to be their position,” he told the Washington Post.
Top tech executives, such as Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, are expected to come under the microscope with Democrats firmly entrenched in power in Washington.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk, a major Republican donor, wrote on X, referring to one of his pet projects at SpaceX.
Meanwhile, Democratic Rep. Greg Casar, head of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, wrote on X that “AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath.”
“The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics,” Casar said.

SPY rose in five of six Novembers after midterms, gaining as much as 6% in 2002 and 2022 following severe bear markets.
DIA finished higher in all six post-midterm years, with gains ranging from 5% to 20%, fitting a broader presidential-cycle pattern.
In 2018, SPY gained nearly 2% in November then crashed 9% in December, ending the year 7% below pre-election levels.

Election nights tend to rattle retirement savers, but Wall Street opened Wednesday more calmly. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ), the most widely held stand-in for the benchmark S&P 500, traded at $763.08 before the open on November 4. That was up 1.16% from its November 3 close of $754.35. Reuters reported that stocks rallied and the dollar dipped after what it called a Democratic midterm sweep. But one session tells a 401(k) holder very little. The more useful guide is how the index behaved in the weeks and months after past midterms. That record shows a steady winning run, along with a few sharp breaks.
SPY's monthly adjusted prices add dividends back in and go back to December 1999. That covers six full midterm cycles. The table compares SPY's October close just before each vote with its November close just after. The index rose in five of the six Novembers and finished flat in the sixth.
The 2002 and 2022 cycles stand out. Both followed severe bear markets, and in each case SPY rallied after the vote. SPY rose more than 5% in November in both years. The worst case was 2010, when the index closed in November exactly where it closed in October.

The Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now
24/7 Wall St has helped investors make money for over two decades, and our top analysts just finished ranking the definitive Top 10 Stocks To Buy Now . Not the ten biggest companies. Not the ten everyone is arguing about. The ten best stocks to buy right now.
The report is free, and you can see why we think each stock is a top investment today.
Enter Your Email and See the Ten →
The longer view is even more consistent. The SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:DIA ) tracks the Dow Jones Industrial Average. It finished higher in all six cycles since 2002, measured from the October close before each vote to the November close a year later. The smallest gain was 4.8% after the 2014 vote and the largest was 20.0% after 2002. In between came 13.9% after 2006, 11.2% after 2010, 14.6% after 2018, and 12.4% after 2022. That run fits a pattern we have tracked before: the year after a midterm has historically been one of the better periods of the four-year presidential cycle.
For anyone near retirement, there is a catch: even the good years came with painful setbacks. In 2018, SPY gained 1.9% in November, then fell 8.8% in December alone. It ended the year at an adjusted 222.8902, which was 7.1% below its level before the election. December also gave back most or all of November's gains in 2002 and 2022.
Even the 12-month periods that ended higher had real turbulence along the way. From November 2018 through October 2019, SPY returned 12.2%, yet at one point it sat 8.8% below its prior peak. From November 2022 through October 2023, SPY returned 4.2% and included an 8.3% drop. From November 2014 through October 2015, SPY returned just 2.4% and fell 8.5% between July and September 2015. In each of those three years, the post-midterm lift came with at least one drop of more than 8%.
This cycle starts from a higher level than most. SPY began Wednesday up 11.9% for the year and 265.9% over 10 years. Still, it went into the vote down 0.86% for the week and 0.85% for the month. The technology-packed Nasdaq-100 has been choppier. The Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) hit $762.86 in October but ended the month at $690.49, 9.5% below that peak. It closed at $685.28 on November 3.
Early sector responses point to rotation, with groups moving in different directions. The Wall Street Journal reported that defense stocks sold off after Democrats' midterm gains. A change in congressional control can reshape spending priorities, and the sectors most tied to Washington tend to adjust first, before broad index funds feel much of the shift.
Over the long run, Wall Street has tended to come out stronger after midterms. The Dow ETF's six-for-six record a year out backs that up. The shorter-term lesson from 2018 is that a strong November can turn into a rough December. I'm watching whether SPY holds above its October close of $755.72 through year-end. Falling below the pre-election October close is exactly what happened in December 2018. For index fund and 401(k) holders, the record points to a positive year ahead, with at least one sharp drop likely along the way (a drawdown early in retirement does far more damage than one later on, which is the whole subject of our free guide on defending the first five years: The First Five Years).

articles.title_orig: SpaceX, Tesla stocks sink as analyst warns Democrats' victory will create 'major hurdles' for AI build-out
articles.title_zh: SpaceX, Tesla stocks sink as analyst warns Democrats' victory will create 'major hurdles' for AI build-out
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
One of Wall Street's biggest AI bulls says the sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections will slow the pace of the AI data center build-out in the US over the next two years. AI-related stocks dropped on Wednesday, including Elon Musk-led SpaceX ( SPCX ) and EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ), which fell 4% before trimming losses as the rest of the market surged.
Shares of cloud provider CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and data center-related companies IREN ( IREN ) and Vertiv ( VRT ) also traded lower on Wednesday after Democrats won a majority in the House and Senate on Tuesday night and flipped governorships across key states.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," Yorkville's partner and managing director, Dan Ives, wrote on Wednesday.
Those hurdles, Ives said, will slow the pace of 800 to 1,000 planned AI data centers across the US. The analyst pointed out that the biggest worry for tech investors and the AI trade is the state of Texas, where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas Governor race over incumbent Greg Abbott in a surprise result. While Abbott currently has a moratorium on data centers in Texas, the prevailing view was that it would have ended were he reelected.
"Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout, which makes worries around the future of the data center buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors," Ives said.
This poses a problem for companies like Texas-based SpaceX, which has been building out its AI infrastructure and taking steps toward a potential merger with Tesla.
"SpaceX and Musk are clearly caught front and center in this spiderweb," said Ives.
"There will be a lot of negotiations and politics on this front especially in Texas which is the foundation of the AI buildout in the US … and Big Tech will need to embrace this new political landscape as of today," he added.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk wrote on X following the election results.
Data center concerns emerged as a key issue in the 2026 midterm elections, with candidates facing growing public opposition to proposed facility locations, the expansion of power infrastructure needed to support them, and concerns that rising electricity demand could drive up consumer costs.
One silver lining for investors may be that political headwinds will force a slowdown in AI capex. AI-related jitters have already weighed on the Tech sector ( XLK ) in recent weeks, with financing concerns hitting neocloud providers that rent out computing capacity, while semiconductor stocks have also retreated.
Long-term, however, Ives remains bullish on the AI trade, as "the Street still is way underestimating the future revenue growth and profitability" stemming from AI.
Fundstrat's Tom Lee is also largely optimistic despite the blue wave.
"President Trump exercises veto power vs any potential 'anti-AI' 'anti-data center' bills," Lee wrote in a note on Tuesday prior to the election results. He also noted that Democrats would likely embrace AI data centers because they bring money and jobs to a community.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Bonds Hit New Lows as Texas Data Centers in Crosshairs
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Bonds Hit New Lows as Texas Data Centers in Crosshairs
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence data center boom hit a roadblock on election night , further complicating the tech industry's historic expansion plans.
There were 41 local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, according to Ballotpedia .
Voters sided against data centers in each measure except one in Harwood, North Dakota, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday.
The City of Harwood voted against a charter rule amendment that would have required additional review before city approval of industrial developments, including data centers.
In Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown ousted Republican Sen. Jon Husted after casting the incumbent as "the face of data centers," 21 local measures were up for a vote, according to Ballotpedia.
The Buckeye State, which was named America's Top State for Business in 2026 by CNBC, has become a key battleground for the issue.
OpenAI announced in August that it secured 8 gigawatts of computing capacity at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, the largest planned AI data center campus in the world. The first phase of construction is slated to begin this year, and capacity is expected to come online in phases starting in 2028, according to the project's website .
SoftBank and SB Energy are developing the Ohio data center campus in partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy. SoftBank is a major investor in OpenAI, and the two companies announced plans to invest $1 billion in SB Energy earlier this year.
Nvidia is also backstopping the project, which could cost more than $500 billion in total.
The Ohio Governor's Mansion also turned blue, as Democrat Amy Acton, a physician, defeated Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy. Acton supports a "conditional moratorium" on data centers to ensure they cover 100% of utility costs and "exclusively build with union labor."
Heading into the election, the AI trade was already faltering on Wall Street, with chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies selling off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. The hyperscalers — Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft and Meta — are each spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on AI infrastructure to meet what they say is insatiable demand. All of those companies except Microsoft have turned cash flow negative in the process.
Getting data center projects off the ground may have just gotten a lot harder.
Communities in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, New Jersey, Nevada and Wisconsin also went to the polls to weigh in on the issue, according to Ballotpedia, and data centers were a key motivating factor for voters in matters up and down the ballot.
In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans.
Democrats who campaigned on pausing or regulating new projects won key races in Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia and Texas, which is on track to become the world's largest data center market by 2030.
In one of the biggest results of the night for Democrats, Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott after blaming the Republican incumbent for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, and putting the tech industry's interests ahead of local communities.
Silicon Valley spent record sums trying to shape the 2026 midterms, with the GOP boasting a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans almost exclusively. Crypto, AI, and online gambling interests poured in more than $377 million.
Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions of dollars this election cycle, largely came up empty.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote in a post on X.
The Texas results appear to be a warning sign for the AI industry as a whole.
Within hours of the polls closing, Democrats were already calling for AI executives to testify under oath.
Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
"The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath."
Casar also accused Republicans of being "bought and paid for by AI billionaires," arguing that voters had rejected that influence and warning Democrats to "hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks."
He said the data center fight is only the beginning.
"The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election," he said. "And in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics."
—CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

Crude oil inventories in the United States saw a decrease of 900,000 barrels during the week ending October 30, according to new data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) released on Wednesday. The decrease brings commercial stockpiles to 409.8 million barrels, according to government data, which is now 4% below the five-year average for this time of year.
Total commercial petroleum inventories slipped by 8.2 million barrels during the reporting period.
The EIA’s data release follows API’s figures that were released a day earlier, which reported that crude oil inventories had fallen by 5.267 million barrels in the period.
Crude futures were trading down at 10:09 a.m. in New York. Brent futures were trading down at $100.71 per barrel—down $2.89 (-2.79%) on the day and down roughly $15 per barrel from this same time last week. WTI was also trading down on the day, by $2.79 per barrel (-2.90%) on Wednesday morning at $93.30 , down nearly $9 per barrel since this time last week.
For total motor gasoline, the EIA reported that inventories decreased by 200,000 barrels, after growing by 3.9 million barrels in the week prior. The most recent figures showed that average daily gasoline production increased to 9.7 million barrels. For middle distillates, inventories decreased by 3.6 million with production decreasing to an average of 5.2 million barrels daily. Distillate inventories are now 13% below the five-year average.
Total products supplied—a proxy for U.S. oil demand—jumped to a 4 week average of 21.2 million barrels per day over the last four weeks, up 4.2% compared to the same period last year. Gasoline demand averaged 8.6 million barrels per day over the last four weeks, with the distillate four-week average supplied at 4.2 million barrels—up 8.7% year over year.
